entries.name: Asleep in the car seat
aliases: can baby sleep in the car seat
entries.why: Asleep in a correctly fitted seat while you are driving is fine. The risk is the seat used as a bed, because the slope lets the head fall forward and squash the airway.
entries.whatToDo: When you arrive, lift them out and lay them flat on their back in the cot or bassinet, even if it wakes them. Check their head position whenever you stop on a long drive.

entries.name: Asleep on your chest
entries.why: Chest naps while you are properly awake and sitting up are lovely and very common. The danger is you dozing off, which Red Nose says never to do with bub on your chest.
entries.whatToDo: Enjoy it while you are awake and upright. The moment you feel yourself going, put them down on their back in the cot or bassinet, or hand them to someone awake.

entries.name: Baby in your bed
entries.why: Red Nose does not recommend bed sharing, but it is honest that it happens, so it publishes a safer position instead of just saying no. Some situations make it never safe.
entries.whatToDo: Use the safer setup below if bub ends up in your bed, and still aim to get them back into their own bassinet beside you. To talk it through, ring Red Nose on 1300 998 698.

variants.label: If you are going to bed share anyway
variants.why: Red Nose gives a safer position: bub on their back, on a firm flat mattress, beside one parent rather than between two adults, and never asleep on your chest.
variants.whatToDo: Bed away from the wall, adult pillows and bedding well clear of their face, no other children or pets in the bed, long hair tied back and jewellery off.

variants.label: Times it is never safe
variants.why: Red Nose says do not bed share at all if anyone in the bed has had alcohol or drowsy medication, smokes, is unwell or very overtired, or if bub was premature or small.
variants.whatToDo: Put bub in their own bassinet beside you instead. If you are too tired to stay awake for a feed, wake the other adult or feed sitting up in bed, never on the couch.

variants.label: Just for the odd night
variants.why: There is no version of bed sharing that is as safe as their own cot, so an occasional night still needs the full safer setup, not a relaxed one.
variants.whatToDo: Same rules every time: on the back, beside one parent, firm flat mattress, bedding and pillows clear. No wrap and no sleeping bag in an adult bed.

entries.name: Back sleeping, every sleep
aliases: which way do i put baby down
entries.why: On the back, every sleep, day and night, until their first birthday. It keeps the airway clear and lets their waking reflexes do their job. Not the side, not the tummy.
entries.whatToDo: Lay bub flat on their back with their feet at the bottom of the cot. If you find them another way, put them back on their back until they can roll both ways on their own.

entries.name: Blankets, pillows and doonas
entries.why: Pillows, doonas, quilts, lambswool and loose blankets can cover the face or cause overheating. A bare cot looks mean and it is the safest cot there is.
entries.whatToDo: Clear it out now. Use firmly tucked lightweight layers, or a fitted sleeping bag and no blanket at all. No pillow until well past their first birthday.

entries.name: Catnapping and 40 minute naps
entries.why: A newborn sleep cycle runs about 40 minutes, so a 30 or 40 minute nap is one full cycle and nothing is broken. Catnapping is a stage, not a habit you taught them by accident.
entries.whatToDo: Try resettling for about 10 minutes before you give up, and stack naps where you can. If they are happy on short sleeps, let the sleeps be short.

entries.name: Days and nights mixed up
aliases: baby awake all night asleep all day
baby has days and nights the wrong way round
entries.why: Newborns are not born with a body clock. The part of the brain that sorts day from night does not really switch on until around 2 to 3 months, so this does fix itself.
entries.whatToDo: Days bright, chatty and noisy as usual. Nights dark, quiet and deeply boring, with feeds and changes done at minimum fuss. Give it a few weeks.

entries.name: Dummies for sleep
aliases: should i use a dummy at sleep time
entries.why: Evidence suggests a dummy used for every sleep may lower the risk of sudden infant death. The question that actually depends is the timing, and that is about breastfeeding.
entries.whatToDo: If you use one, use it for every sleep rather than some. Never force it on a baby who spits it out, and never dip it in anything sweet.

variants.label: Breastfed and under about 4 to 6 weeks
variants.why: Red Nose says wait until breastfeeding is established, usually around four to six weeks, so the dummy does not get in the way of supply and attachment.
variants.whatToDo: Hold off for now and settle with a cuddle, a wrap or a rock. Ring the ABA helpline if feeding is already hard going.

variants.label: Breastfeeding established, or bottle fed
variants.why: Go ahead. Offer it at the start of every sleep, and if it drops out once they are asleep there is no need to go back in and replace it.
variants.whatToDo: A one piece dummy meeting the Australian standard, checked for splits and replaced regularly. Phase it out somewhere between two and four years.

entries.name: Falling asleep on the couch or in an armchair
aliases: fell asleep on the couch with baby
entries.why: This is the one Red Nose calls extremely dangerous with no safe version. Couches and recliners have gaps and soft cushions a baby's face wedges into, and you will not feel it happen.
entries.whatToDo: Move now, and every time. If you feed at night and might nod off, do it sitting up in bed with the bedding pushed back, not on the couch or in a recliner.

entries.name: How much sleep they need
aliases: how much sleep does a baby need
entries.why: Totals are an average across the whole 24 hours, not a target, and the spread between perfectly normal babies is enormous. Watch the baby, not the chart.
entries.whatToDo: If they are feeding well, wetting nappies, growing and happy for some part of the day, the number on the chart does not matter much.

variants.label: Newborn, 0 to 3 months
variants.why: Usually 14 to 17 hours across the day and night, in grabs of 2 to 4 hours, with no sense of day or night yet. Sleep cycles are only about 40 minutes long.
variants.whatToDo: Sleep when you can rather than chasing a routine. Feed on demand, day and night.

variants.label: 3 to 6 months
variants.why: Around 12 to 15 hours in 24, with night sleep starting to pull together into longer stretches plus a few day naps. Most babies at this age still wake overnight.
variants.whatToDo: A loose feed, play, sleep rhythm and a short wind-down helps more than a strict clock.

variants.label: 6 to 12 months
variants.why: Roughly 11 to 14 hours in 24, usually two naps and a longer night. Plenty still wake once or more, and crawling or pulling to stand can scramble it for weeks.
variants.whatToDo: Keep bedtime predictable and boring. If it has been bad for weeks, your MCH nurse can help or refer you on.

entries.name: How to resettle
aliases: how do i resettle my baby
entries.why: A short wake at the end of a sleep cycle often needs very little. A hand on the chest and a quiet voice resettles plenty of babies before they are properly awake.
entries.whatToDo: Go in quietly, lights off, hand on the chest or gentle patting, no conversation. Give it about 10 minutes before you pick them up or feed them.

entries.name: Own cot, in your room
aliases: can baby sleep in our room
entries.why: Red Nose says own cot or bassinet, in your room, for at least the first six months. Sharing the room lowers the risk. Sharing the bed is a separate question.
entries.whatToDo: Set the bassinet beside your bed, within arm's reach, on its own firm flat mattress. Keep it there until at least six months, longer if it suits you.

entries.name: Reducing the risk of SIDS
aliases: how do i reduce the risk of sids
entries.why: You cannot get the risk to zero, but the six things Red Nose lists do most of the work, and they are all small practical changes rather than constant vigilance.
entries.whatToDo: Back to sleep every sleep. Head and face uncovered. Smoke free before and after birth. Safe sleep space day and night. Own cot in your room for six months. Breastfeed if you can.

entries.name: Sleep regressions
entries.why: Around four months sleep genuinely reorganises, so a baby who slept beautifully can start waking lots. Later blips usually line up with rolling, crawling or standing.
entries.whatToDo: Hold your routine steady and resettle the way you normally would. It generally settles within a couple of weeks. Try not to start habits you will have to undo.

entries.name: Sleeping bags
entries.why: A properly fitted sleeping bag is Red Nose's easiest answer to loose bedding, because it cannot ride up over the face. The catch is the fit and the warmth.
entries.whatToDo: Fitted neck and armholes, no hood, and the right weight for the room. Nothing else goes over the top of it.

variants.label: Right size, fitted neck, no hood
variants.why: This is the setup Red Nose likes. It stays put, the head stays clear, and you do not have to tuck anything in at 3am.
variants.whatToDo: Match the TOG to the room, dress bub lightly underneath, and skip blankets entirely.

variants.label: Too big, hooded, or a blanket on top
variants.why: A loose neck or armhole lets bub slip down inside the bag, a hood can cover the face, and a blanket over the top is an overheating risk.
variants.whatToDo: Change it tonight for a bag that fits the neck and arms snugly with no hood, and take the extra blanket off.

entries.name: Swaddling and wrapping
entries.why: Wrapping helps a lot of newborns settle on their back, and Red Nose is fine with it done properly. Whether it is still right depends on how close bub is to rolling.
entries.whatToDo: Light cotton or muslin, firm but not tight, room to move the hips and chest, and never wrapped higher than the shoulders.

variants.label: Newborn, no sign of rolling
variants.why: Wrap away. A firm light wrap settles plenty of newborns and helps them stay on their back, which is exactly where you want them.
variants.whatToDo: Lightweight cotton or muslin, not a bunny rug or blanket. Shoulders down only, hips free to bend up and out, face and head uncovered.

variants.label: Any sign of rolling, or about 3 months
variants.why: Red Nose says stop wrapping as soon as they show signs of rolling or reach about 3 months, whichever comes first. A wrapped baby who rolls cannot get their arms out.
variants.whatToDo: Swap to a fitted sleeping bag with armholes tonight. Expect a few unsettled nights while they get used to having their arms free.

variants.label: In a sleeping bag, or sharing a sleep surface
variants.why: Red Nose says do not wrap a baby who is in a sleeping bag, or who is sharing a sleep surface with anyone. The two together add up to too much.
variants.whatToDo: Pick one: a firm wrap in their own cot, or a sleeping bag. Never both, and no wrap at all in an adult bed.

entries.name: The witching hour at bedtime
entries.why: Most newborn fussing lands in the late afternoon and evening, and crying peaks around 6 to 8 weeks before it eases off. It is not something either of you caused.
entries.whatToDo: Ride it out in shifts. A walk, a bath, skin to skin, a dark quiet room or a carrier each help some babies. Hand over before you run out of patience, not after.

entries.name: They rolled onto their tummy
aliases: baby rolled onto tummy in sleep
entries.why: Rolling is a milestone, not a mistake. What matters is whether they can get themselves back, and what is in the cot with them when they do.
entries.whatToDo: Keep starting every sleep on the back, and clear everything soft out of the cot so there is nothing to roll into.

variants.label: Cannot roll back yet
variants.why: If they roll to their front and get stuck there, that is the risky position. Keep starting every sleep on the back and keep the cot completely bare.
variants.whatToDo: Roll them gently back onto their back. Stop wrapping now and use a fitted sleeping bag instead, so their arms are free to help them.

variants.label: Rolls both ways confidently
variants.why: Once they can roll both directions on their own, you can leave them in whatever position they end up in. You still start them on their back.
variants.whatToDo: Keep the cot free of pillows, bumpers, soft toys and loose bedding, because now they can get to it.

entries.name: Too hot
entries.why: Overheating raises the risk of sudden infant death. Hands and feet run cool on every baby, so they tell you nothing. The chest and the back of the neck are the honest test.
entries.whatToDo: Slip a hand on their chest or the back of their neck. Clammy or hot means take a layer off now. Keep the head uncovered and move the cot out of direct sun.

entries.name: Tummy or side sleeping
entries.why: Tummy and side sleeping both raise the risk of sudden infant death, and side is not a safe halfway house because they tip onto their front. Better sleep is not worth it.
entries.whatToDo: Change it tonight: always place them on their back. If they settle badly that way, try a firm light wrap or a dummy rather than the tummy.

entries.name: Waking all night
aliases: why does my baby keep waking up
entries.why: Waking at night is how babies are built: small stomachs, short sleep cycles, and a brief wake at the end of each one. At six months plenty still wake once or more.
entries.whatToDo: Feed or resettle, keep it dark and dull, and get back to bed. Take turns so at least one of you gets a real block of sleep each night.

entries.name: What to dress them in
aliases: what should baby wear to bed
entries.why: Roughly what you would wear to bed, plus one light layer, is the usual rule of thumb. The point is a head that stays uncovered and a chest that feels comfortably warm.
entries.whatToDo: A singlet and a cotton suit under a sleeping bag suits most nights. Lighter TOG in summer, heavier in winter. No hat, no hood, no blanket over the bag.

entries.name: When to stop swaddling
entries.why: The cut-off is the first sign of rolling, or around 3 months, whichever comes first. Not when they seem ready, and not when the sleep finally gets good.
entries.whatToDo: Move to a fitted sleeping bag with armholes now. Cold turkey or one arm out at a time both work. Keep starting every sleep on the back.

entries.name: You are at the end of your rope
aliases: i have not slept in days
at the end of my rope from no sleep
entries.why: You have been awake too long and you are running on nothing. That is not weakness and it is not a parenting failure. It is the point where another adult needs to be involved.
entries.whatToDo: Put bub on their back in their cot, shut the door and breathe. Then ring your MCH nurse today, or PANDA on 1300 726 306. If you are frightened of what you might do, ring 000.

entries.name: You fell asleep feeding in bed
aliases: i fell asleep feeding in bed
woke up with baby in bed
entries.why: It happens to most people, and panicking about it afterwards does not help. What helps is setting the bed up first, so if you do doze off bub is already in the safer position.
entries.whatToDo: Before the feed, push pillows and doonas well clear, move the bed off the wall, and feed with bub beside you rather than between you two. Then put them back in the bassinet.

entries.name: Asleep in the pram
aliases: can baby sleep in the pram
entries.why: Pram naps happen, and a flat pram bassinet is a reasonable short sleep. An upright or part-reclined pram seat is not, because the head can slump forward onto the chest.
entries.whatToDo: Lie the pram flat if it does, keep bub on their back, check on them often, and move them to the cot for the long sleeps once you are home.

entries.name: Baby monitors and breathing mats
entries.why: Monitors are handy for hearing bub, but no monitor, mat or sock has been shown to prevent sudden infant death. They can give false comfort and tempt you to skip the basics.
entries.whatToDo: Use one if you like it, but do not trade it for a safe sleep setup. Back sleeping, bare cot and their own bed in your room are the parts that actually work.

entries.name: Breathing oddly, blue or grey
entries.why: Pauses with a colour change, grunting on every breath, ribs sucking in, or blue or grey lips, tongue or face are urgent. Brief pauses in a pink, settled newborn are different.
entries.whatToDo: If they are blue, grey, floppy or working hard for every breath, ring 000 now. Keep them on their back and stay with them until help arrives.

entries.name: Cot bumpers
entries.why: Cot bumpers are not safe. They have been involved in fatal sleep accidents, and padding the cot sides does not prevent any injury worth that risk.
entries.whatToDo: Take them out tonight, ties and all. If bub is knocking an arm or a leg on the rails, that is normal and it does not hurt them.

entries.name: Dark rooms and night lights
aliases: does baby need a night light
entries.why: Dark helps at night, and babies are not generally frightened of it. Darkened daytime naps are fine too, as long as the rest of the day still feels like day.
entries.whatToDo: Dark and quiet at night, with a dim lamp for feeds rather than the big light. Keep daytime bright and sociable so the body clock gets the message.

entries.name: Dummy keeps falling out
aliases: do i put the dummy back in
entries.why: Falling out is what dummies do, and you are not required to run an overnight dummy service. Red Nose says if it drops out once bub is asleep, just leave it.
entries.whatToDo: Offer it as they go down, then let it go. If you are up five times a night putting it back, that is the sign to stop offering it at that sleep.

entries.name: Feet to foot of the cot
aliases: where in the cot do i put baby
entries.why: Sleep them with their feet at the bottom end of the cot so they cannot wriggle down under the covers. That is how the head and face stay uncovered.
entries.whatToDo: Feet to the foot of the cot, blankets tucked in firmly no higher than chest level, arms out over the top. A fitted sleeping bag does the same job with less fuss.

entries.name: Firm, flat mattress
entries.why: A mattress needs to be firm, flat and the right size for the cot. Soft or saggy surfaces let the face sink in, and gaps at the edges can trap a head or a limb.
entries.whatToDo: Press it: it should not dip under your hand. Keep the gap around the edges under 20mm. Never add a soft topper, sheepskin or extra padding.

entries.name: Getting real help with sleep
aliases: where can i get help with baby sleep
entries.why: There is proper help in Australia and you do not have to be desperate to use it. Early parenting centres, often called sleep schools, run day stays and residential stays.
entries.whatToDo: Start with your MCH nurse or GP, who can rule out a health cause and refer you. The MCH Line on 13 22 29 can point you at your nearest early parenting centre, any hour.

entries.name: Hard to wake, floppy or not feeding
entries.why: A baby who will not wake properly, has gone floppy, or will not feed needs to be seen straight away. This is not something to watch and see about in the morning.
entries.whatToDo: Ring 000 now. Stay with them, keep them on their back, and tell the operator how old they are and how long they have been like this.

entries.name: Head and face covered
aliases: should baby wear a hat to sleep
entries.why: Babies shed heat through the head and face, so both stay uncovered for sleep. A hat, a hood or bedding over the face stops them cooling themselves down.
entries.whatToDo: Uncover the head now. No hats or beanies indoors for sleep, no hooded sleeping bags, and bedding tucked no higher than the chest.

entries.name: How long in the capsule
aliases: how long can baby stay in the capsule
entries.why: There is no official Australian number, but the sensible habit is short stretches and regular breaks. Red Nose is clear a capsule is not a sleep space once you have arrived.
entries.whatToDo: On long drives, stop every couple of hours, take them out, and let them lie flat for a while. At home, straight out of the capsule and into the cot.

entries.name: Is this cot safe
entries.why: A cot needs to meet the Australian standard AS/NZS 2172, with the right bar spacing and no gaps the mattress leaves open. Old, broken or drop-side cots are not safe.
entries.whatToDo: Look for the standards label and check every bolt is tight. Skip anything with cut-outs, peeling paint or a drop side. Secondhand is fine if it still meets the standard.

entries.name: Positioners, nests and inclined sleepers
entries.why: Positioners, wedges, nests, hammocks and anything that props bub on a slope are not recommended for sleep. A sloped or padded surface lets the chin drop and the airway close.
entries.whatToDo: Move them to a flat firm cot or bassinet for sleep, tonight. If you were sold one for reflux, ring your nurse or GP before you use it again.

entries.name: Premature or small babies
aliases: safe sleep for a premature baby
entries.why: Premature and small babies carry a higher risk, so the safe sleep rules matter more, not less. Red Nose says never bed share with a baby who was premature or small for dates.
entries.whatToDo: Own cot in your room, on the back, bare cot, no bed sharing. Age markers like comforters at 7 months go by corrected age. Follow the plan the hospital sent you home with.

entries.name: Putting a wrap over the pram
aliases: can i put a muslin over the pram
covering the pram with a wrap
entries.why: A cloth over the pram, even a thin muslin, cuts the airflow and traps heat. Red Nose cites testing where a covered pram got almost four degrees hotter inside.
entries.whatToDo: Take it off. Use the pram's own canopy, a clip-on shade that does not sit across the opening, real shade, or just head out at a cooler time of day.

entries.name: Room temperature
aliases: what temperature should the room be
entries.why: There is no magic number. Red Nose says no particular room temperature has been shown to prevent sudden infant death, so dress bub for the room you actually have.
entries.whatToDo: Aim for a room you would sleep in comfortably yourself. Feel their chest or the back of their neck, and add or drop a layer based on that, not on a gauge.

entries.name: Self-settling
aliases: how do i teach self settling
entries.why: Self-settling is a skill that turns up with development, not something you can drill into a newborn. What is reasonable depends almost entirely on age.
entries.whatToDo: Put them down drowsy but awake when you can, and help them when they need it. Both of those are allowed on the same night.

variants.label: Under 6 months
variants.why: Newborns and young babies need you to settle them, and responding does not spoil anything. Try putting them down drowsy but awake, then step in if that does not work.
variants.whatToDo: Settle in arms, or hands on in the cot with patting and a calm voice. Red Nose rules still apply: on the back, own cot, nothing soft in with them.

variants.label: 6 to 18 months
variants.why: From about six months you can start easing off the help in small steps, so they get practice falling asleep in the cot rather than in your arms.
variants.whatToDo: Reduce one bit of help at a time, or try camping out, where you sit beside the cot and move further away over a week or two.

entries.name: Sleep props and associations
aliases: baby will only sleep if i feed them
entries.why: A sleep association is just whatever bub expects at the moment of falling asleep: feeding, rocking, a dummy, you. It is not damage, and it can be changed later on.
entries.whatToDo: For now, use whatever gets everybody sleeping. If a prop stops working for you, phase it out in small steps rather than all at once.

entries.name: Sleeping too long to feed
aliases: should i wake baby to feed
entries.why: A long sleep is usually a gift, but a brand new baby who is very sleepy and skipping feeds needs watching. Weight gain and wet nappies are the things to check.
entries.whatToDo: Unless your nurse or GP told you to wake them for feeds, you generally need not. If they are jaundiced, losing weight or feeding poorly, ring your MCH nurse today.

entries.name: Smoking and vaping around bub
entries.why: Smoke exposure before or after birth is one of the biggest risk factors for sudden infant death, and babies around smoke do not rouse as easily. Smoking outside still counts.
entries.whatToDo: Keep the house and the car smoke free, change clothes and wash hands before cuddles, and never bed share if anyone in the bed smokes. Quitting at any point still helps.

entries.name: Soft toys and comforters
aliases: can baby sleep with a comforter
entries.why: Soft toys and comforters in the sleep space come down to age. For a young baby they are a suffocation risk and they do not belong in the cot at all.
entries.whatToDo: Keep the cot bare for now. If you want a comforter later, pick a small flat one with no beads, buttons or long ribbons.

variants.label: Under about 7 months
variants.why: Red Nose says no soft toys or comforters in the sleep space until at least 7 months, corrected for prematurity. Younger babies cannot shift something off their own face.
variants.whatToDo: Take it out of the cot tonight. Use it for cuddles while they are awake instead.

variants.label: About 7 months or older
variants.why: From around 7 months, corrected for prematurity, one small comforter in the cot is generally fine, and it can be a real help at bedtime.
variants.whatToDo: One small flat comforter, nothing with beads, batteries, buttons or ribbons. Keep the rest of the cot clear.

entries.name: White noise
aliases: does white noise actually help sleep
entries.why: White noise calms a lot of babies and there is nothing unsafe about it in itself. It just becomes one of the things they expect for sleep, which is no great problem.
entries.whatToDo: Keep it quiet enough that you can talk over it, and the speaker well away from the cot, never inside it. A fan or a radio off station does the same job.

entries.name: Wrap too tight, or arms zipped in
entries.why: A loose wrap turns into loose bedding, and a tight one squashes the hips and chest. Red Nose also says never use a swaddle that pins the arms down with velcro or zips.
entries.whatToDo: You should fit a flat hand between the wrap and their chest, and their legs should still bend up and out. Wrap from the shoulders down, never over the head or face.

entries.name: Dream feeds
aliases: should i do a dream feed
late evening top up before bed
entries.why: A dream feed is a feed you offer late in the evening without properly waking bub. It works nicely for some families and does nothing at all for others. It is optional.
entries.whatToDo: Try it for a week and see. If it buys you a longer first stretch, keep it. If it just wakes everybody up, drop it and feel no guilt.

entries.name: Attachment and latch
aliases: how do i know the latch is right
baby keeps slipping off the breast
entries.why: A good attachment feels like firm tugging, not pinching or biting. Chin in first, nose clear, a big mouthful of breast, more areola showing above the top lip than below, no clicking.
entries.whatToDo: If it hurts, break the seal with a clean finger and start again rather than pushing on. One face to face session with an ABA counsellor or lactation consultant fixes most of it.

entries.name: Cluster feeding
entries.why: Hours of back to back feeding, usually late afternoon or evening, is normal newborn behaviour. It is not a sign you have run out of milk. It often lines up with a growth spurt.
entries.whatToDo: Park yourself somewhere comfortable with water, snacks and a charger, and let it happen. Hand the baby over between feeds if there is someone to hand them to.

entries.name: Falling asleep at the breast
aliases: wakes up the second i put him down
entries.why: Most newborns doze off at the breast. Warm milk, warm body, job done. It only matters if they keep falling asleep before they have taken a decent feed.
entries.whatToDo: Try breast compressions, a nappy change or taking a layer off to rouse them. If feeds stay short and wet nappies drop off, ring the ABA helpline on 1800 686 268.

entries.name: Fewer wet nappies than expected
entries.why: Fewer wet nappies than expected can mean your baby is not getting enough milk. In a newborn that can change quickly, so this is a today thing, not a tomorrow thing.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP or MCH nurse now. If your baby also seems sleepy, floppy or hard to wake, go straight to an emergency department.

entries.name: How often a newborn feeds
aliases: how often should a newborn feed
is my baby feeding too much
entries.why: Newborns feed 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, sometimes more, and almost never on a tidy schedule. Tiny stomach, fast digestion. Feeding whenever they ask is how your supply gets built.
entries.whatToDo: Feed on early cues: stirring, hands to mouth, turning towards you. Crying is a late cue. Count feeds across the whole day rather than measuring the gaps.

entries.name: How to tell your baby is getting enough
aliases: how do i know my baby is getting enough milk
entries.why: You cannot measure a breast, so you measure the baby. Heavy wet nappies, steady weight gain, alert awake periods and swallowing you can hear are what actually tell you.
entries.whatToDo: From about day 5, look for six or more heavy wet nappies in 24 hours, plus regular weight checks with your MCH nurse. Stop counting minutes on the clock.

entries.name: Making up formula safely
entries.why: Formula powder is not sterile, so how you make it up matters much more than which brand you bought. Water, order and timing are the whole job.
entries.whatToDo: Boil water and let it cool, pour the water in first, then add level scoops with the tin's own scoop. Make it fresh for each feed and tip out what is left after an hour.

entries.name: Night feeds
aliases: feeding every two hours at night
do i have to feed at night
entries.why: Night feeds are normal and necessary for months, and the hormone that builds supply runs highest overnight. A newborn stomach simply cannot stretch to a whole night.
entries.whatToDo: Set up a feeding spot with water, a dim light and nappy gear in reach. Split the night between you rather than both being awake for all of it.

entries.name: Posseting or vomiting
aliases: is that spit up or vomit
how much spit up is normal
entries.why: A mouthful of milk coming back up after a feed is posseting, and most babies do it. Vomiting is forceful, bigger, and tends to arrive with other signs.
entries.whatToDo: Look at your baby rather than the muslin. Comfortable, feeding and gaining weight points firmly at posseting.

variants.label: Small spills, happy baby, gaining weight
variants.why: Posseting. It looks like far more milk than it is, and it fades as they grow and spend more of the day upright.
variants.whatToDo: Smaller, more frequent feeds, a bit of upright time afterwards, and a cloth on every shoulder in the house.

variants.label: Vomiting most feeds, or not gaining weight
variants.why: Frequent forceful vomiting alongside poor weight gain is worth a proper look rather than managing at home.
variants.whatToDo: Book with your GP or MCH nurse this week and bring your baby's health record book with the weights in it.

variants.label: Projectile vomit, green or bloody vomit, or an unwell baby
variants.why: These point at something that needs assessing today rather than watching for another day.
variants.whatToDo: See a GP today. Ring 000 if your baby is floppy, hard to wake or struggling to breathe.

entries.name: Reflux
aliases: arches his back and cries after feeds
entries.why: Most babies bring milk up and most of them are untroubled by it. Reflux becomes worth treating when there is real pain, refusing feeds, poor weight gain or ongoing distress.
entries.whatToDo: Smaller feeds more often, upright for a while afterwards. Never tilt the cot mattress or use a wedge: flat on the back is still safest. See your GP if feeds are distressing.

entries.name: Sore, cracked or bleeding nipples
aliases: my nipples hurt when he feeds
entries.why: Tenderness in the first week is common. Cracks, bleeding, or pain that lasts the whole feed are not, and they nearly always point at attachment rather than at you being soft.
entries.whatToDo: Get the attachment checked and ring the ABA helpline on 1800 686 268. Express a drop of milk onto the nipple after feeds and let it air dry. Swallowed blood will not hurt your baby.

entries.name: When solids start
aliases: signs baby is ready for solids
can i start solids at four months
entries.why: Solids start at around 6 months, when your baby can hold their head steady, sit with support, and reach for and mouth food. Milk stays the main event for the whole first year.
entries.whatToDo: Go by the signs rather than the date. Start with one small taste a day after a milk feed, and keep breast milk or formula going until at least 12 months.

entries.name: Wind and burping
entries.why: Babies swallow air and sometimes need a hand getting it back up. Some burp every single time, some never do, and a comfortable baby does not need one chased out of them.
entries.whatToDo: Hold them upright against your shoulder, or sit them on your lap with a hand supporting the chest, and rub or pat gently. Five minutes is plenty, then move on.

entries.name: Worried about low supply
aliases: i dont think i have enough milk
entries.why: Most parents who worry about supply have plenty of milk. Soft breasts, a baby who feeds often, and a let down you cannot feel are not evidence of a problem.
entries.whatToDo: Count wet nappies and look at weight gain. Those two answer the question far better than how full your breasts feel.

variants.label: Nappies and weight are on track
variants.why: Six or more heavy wet nappies a day and steady weight gain mean your baby is getting enough, however empty you feel between feeds.
variants.whatToDo: Keep feeding on demand. You do not need to add formula top ups unless someone has advised them for a specific reason.

variants.label: Fewer wet nappies, slow weight gain, or a baby never satisfied
variants.why: Those are the real signs of a supply problem, and they are much easier to sort out this week than next month.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your MCH nurse for a weigh and a feeding review, and the ABA helpline on 1800 686 268 for hands on help.

entries.name: Alcohol while breastfeeding
aliases: can i have a drink while breastfeeding
entries.why: Alcohol passes into breast milk at roughly the level in your blood, and it clears as your blood clears. Not drinking is safest, and a planned drink can be worked around.
entries.whatToDo: Feed or express first, then allow about two hours per standard drink before the next feed. Pumping and dumping does not speed it up. Never share a sleep surface after drinking.

entries.name: Blocked duct
entries.why: A tender lump that stays put after a feed is usually a blocked duct. A missed feed, a tight bra strap or a shallow attachment are the common causes.
entries.whatToDo: Keep feeding on that side, massage gently towards the nipple, cold packs in between. Fever, chills or a spreading red patch means mastitis, and that needs a GP today.

entries.name: Bottle refusal
aliases: back to work and she wont take a bottle
entries.why: Lots of breastfed babies knock back a bottle at first, especially from the person who usually feeds them. It is a preference, not a protest, and it generally shifts with practice.
entries.whatToDo: Let someone else offer it when your baby is calm rather than starving, try a different teat or temperature, and keep tries short. Cup or spoon feeding works in the meantime.

entries.name: Caffeine while breastfeeding
aliases: how much coffee can i have
is caffeine bad for my baby
entries.why: You can have your coffee. A moderate amount, roughly two or three cups a day, suits most babies fine. A few newborns are sensitive and go a bit wired and wakeful.
entries.whatToDo: Watch your baby rather than the cup count. If they seem jittery or hard to settle, cut back for a week and see. Tea, cola, energy drinks and chocolate all count too.

entries.name: Choking or gagging
entries.why: Gagging is loud, red faced and protective: the reflex pushing food back forward. Choking is quiet, because no air is moving. The noise is actually the reassuring part.
entries.whatToDo: Always feed sitting upright, never in a car seat or on the move, and stay beside your baby for the whole meal.

variants.label: Gagging: coughing, retching, loud, going red
variants.why: This is your baby learning to manage food, and it settles with practice over the next few weeks.
variants.whatToDo: Stay calm and close, keep your fingers out of their mouth, and let them work the food forward themselves.

variants.label: Choking: silent, cannot cough or cry, lips going blue
variants.why: Nothing is getting past the blockage and your baby needs help immediately.
variants.whatToDo: Ring 000 and start first aid now: back blows, then chest thrusts. Do not drive to hospital with a choking baby.

entries.name: Choosing a formula
aliases: do i need a special formula
entries.why: Every infant formula sold in Australia has to meet the same standard, so a stage 1 cow's milk formula from any brand is fine. The expensive tin is not better milk.
entries.whatToDo: Pick a stage 1 formula and stay with it unless there is a medical reason to change. Talk to your GP or MCH nurse before buying goat, soy, HA or anti reflux versions.

entries.name: Combo feeding
entries.why: Plenty of Australian families do some breast and some formula, and it works. Breast milk supply does respond to how much is taken, so expect it to adjust a little.
entries.whatToDo: If you want to protect supply, offer the breast first and keep a few consistent breast feeds a day. Any combination that keeps all of you fed is a good one.

entries.name: Cow's milk
aliases: when can babies have cows milk
entries.why: Plain cow's milk is not suitable as a main drink before 12 months, because it is low in iron and hard on young kidneys. Cow's milk in cooking or as yoghurt from 6 months is fine.
entries.whatToDo: Stay with breast milk or formula until 12 months, then full cream cow's milk is fine. Ask your GP before using plant milks, which can be very low in protein and energy.

entries.name: Dropping night feeds
aliases: when do babies stop feeding at night
entries.why: Some babies drop night feeds themselves in the second half of the first year, once solids and weight gain are well established. There is no age at which they all do it.
entries.whatToDo: Let your baby lead until at least 6 months. Talk to your MCH nurse first if weight gain has been slow, and shorten feeds gradually rather than stopping overnight.

entries.name: Engorgement
aliases: my milk came in and it hurts
entries.why: Around day 3 to 5 your breasts can go hard, hot and tight as the milk comes in. Uncomfortable, usually short lived, and it eases as supply and demand find each other.
entries.whatToDo: Feed often, warmth before a feed and cold packs after. Hand express a little to soften the areola so your baby can attach. Watch for fever or a spreading red patch.

entries.name: Expressing with a pump
entries.why: Pump output is not a supply report. A pump is far less efficient than a baby, and a disappointing number on a tired afternoon means very little.
entries.whatToDo: Check the flange actually fits, pump on comfort rather than maximum, and try after a morning feed when supply runs highest. Wash and dry all parts after every use.

entries.name: Feeding in public
aliases: is it legal to breastfeed in public
entries.why: In Australia you have the legal right to breastfeed wherever you are. Nobody can ask you to leave, move or cover up, and it is protected under federal discrimination law.
entries.whatToDo: Wear something you can get out of easily, have a practice at home if it helps, and sit wherever you like. ABA lists breastfeeding friendly venues if you want a soft start.

entries.name: First foods
entries.why: There is no magic first food. Iron rich ones matter most: meat, chicken, fish, tofu, legumes, eggs and iron fortified cereal, alongside vegetables and fruit.
entries.whatToDo: Offer soft lumpy textures and safe finger foods early rather than months of smooth puree. No added salt or sugar, and no honey before 12 months.

entries.name: Growth spurts
entries.why: Around 3 weeks, 6 weeks and 3 months a lot of babies suddenly feed more, sleep worse and seem permanently unsatisfied. It runs for a few days. It is not your supply failing.
entries.whatToDo: Feed on demand and let the extra feeding do its job of lifting supply. Cancel what you can for a few days and say yes to every offer of food.

entries.name: Hand expressing
entries.why: Your hands are free, always with you, and often better than a pump in the first days when there are only drops of colostrum to collect.
entries.whatToDo: Warm the breast, make a C shape a few centimetres back from the nipple, press back towards your chest, then compress and release in a rhythm. Move around the breast.

entries.name: How long a feed should take
aliases: how long should a feed take
entries.why: Anywhere from about 10 minutes to nearly an hour is normal, and it changes feed to feed. Some babies are brutally efficient, others like a long lunch. Length alone tells you little.
entries.whatToDo: Watch for deep rhythmic swallowing instead of the clock. Let your baby finish one side before you offer the other. Nappies and weight are the real measures.

entries.name: Introducing allergens
entries.why: Australian advice is to introduce the common allergens in the first year, from around 6 months: egg, peanut, tree nuts, dairy, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish and sesame.
entries.whatToDo: Offer a smooth form such as thinned peanut paste, a small amount at home in the daytime, and keep it in the diet regularly. Ask your GP first if there is eczema or family history.

entries.name: Jaundice affecting feeding
entries.why: Mild jaundice in the first week is common. It needs reviewing when your baby is deeply yellow, hard to wake, feeding poorly, or still yellow after two weeks.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP or midwife today for a review and a bilirubin check. Keep offering feeds often, because feeding is what clears it.

entries.name: Leaking milk
aliases: leaking when i hear a baby cry
entries.why: Leaking is very common in the early weeks, often at night or when you hear any baby anywhere cry. It settles as your supply learns the routine. Not leaking is also fine.
entries.whatToDo: Breast pads, dark tops and a towel over the mattress. Press the heel of your hand against the nipple if you need to stop a let down while you are out.

entries.name: Mastitis
aliases: red hot sore breast with fever
feel like i have the flu breastfeeding
entries.why: A red, hot, painful area in the breast along with fever, chills or flu like aching is mastitis. It can move quickly and it usually needs treatment rather than waiting it out.
entries.whatToDo: See a GP today, or tonight if you are getting worse. Keep feeding or expressing from that side. The ABA helpline on 1800 686 268 can help you drain it.

entries.name: Medications while breastfeeding
entries.why: Most common medicines are compatible with breastfeeding, and stopping feeds is rarely the answer. The amount that reaches your milk is usually very small.
entries.whatToDo: Check before you take anything, including over the counter and herbal products: ring your pharmacist or GP. Never stop a prescribed medicine on your own. We never give doses.

entries.name: Paced bottle feeding
entries.why: Holding the bottle closer to level slows the flow, so your baby can pause, breathe and stop when they are full instead of being overtaken by it. It helps with wind too.
entries.whatToDo: Sit them fairly upright, tickle the lip and let them draw the teat in, keep the bottle near horizontal, and take breaks. Never prop a bottle and never push the last bit.

entries.name: Projectile vomiting
entries.why: Vomiting that flies rather than dribbles, especially after most feeds in a baby a few weeks old, needs checking. It can mean the outlet from the stomach is narrowing.
entries.whatToDo: See a GP today. If your baby is also sleepy, floppy, has fewer wet nappies or looks unwell, go to an emergency department or ring 000.

entries.name: Significant weight loss
entries.why: Losing more than about a tenth of birth weight, or not being back to birth weight by around two weeks, means feeding needs reviewing now rather than at the next visit.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP or MCH nurse today for a weigh and a feeding review. Keep feeding often meanwhile, and the ABA helpline on 1800 686 268 can help with the feeding side.

entries.name: Silent reflux
aliases: swallows it back down and cries
no vomit but screams after feeds
entries.why: Some babies swallow the milk back down, so you get the discomfort without the mess. It is the same thing as reflux and it is judged the same way: pain, feeding and weight.
entries.whatToDo: Keep a rough log of feeds, crying and weights for a week and take it to your GP or MCH nurse. Try not to start medicines or swap formulas on guesswork.

entries.name: Sterilising bottles
entries.why: In Australia, bottles, teats and dummies get washed and sterilised for the whole first year. Washing on its own does not do the job.
entries.whatToDo: Scrub in hot soapy water with a bottle brush first, then steam, boil or use a chemical steriliser. Keep sterilised gear covered and wash your hands before assembling it.

entries.name: Storing and warming breast milk
aliases: how long does breast milk last in the fridge
entries.why: Fresh expressed milk keeps a few days in the back of the fridge and months in a deep freezer. Label every container with the date, because you will absolutely forget.
entries.whatToDo: Thaw in the fridge or under cool running water, warm in a jug of warm water, never in the microwave because it makes hot spots. Swirl rather than shake. Do not refreeze.

entries.name: Told to push through the pain
aliases: someone told me to push through the pain
entries.why: Feeding should not be agony, and pushing through is not advice, it is just pain. Something fixable is usually going on: attachment, thrush, a blocked duct, a tongue tie.
entries.whatToDo: Ring the ABA helpline on 1800 686 268. It runs 24 hours a day and they will talk it through with you tonight, not in a fortnight.

entries.name: Tongue tie
entries.why: A tight piece of tissue under the tongue only matters if it is actually causing trouble: pain for you, a shallow latch, clicking, slipping off, or poor weight gain.
entries.whatToDo: Get the feeding assessed first, by an ABA counsellor, a lactation consultant or your GP. Many ties need nothing. If a release is suggested, ask what problem it solves.

entries.name: Too sleepy to feed
aliases: baby wont wake up to feed
hard to wake for a feed
entries.why: A newborn who will not wake for feeds, or who cannot stay awake long enough to take one, needs assessing. Sleepiness can be the first sign that something else is wrong.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP or MCH nurse today. If your baby cannot be roused, is floppy, or has not fed for many hours, ring 000.

entries.name: Water for babies
aliases: how much water for a baby
entries.why: Babies under 6 months do not need water. Breast milk or formula covers all of it, and extra water can fill them up or upset the salt balance in their blood.
entries.whatToDo: From around 6 months offer small amounts of cooled boiled tap water in a cup with meals. Never water down formula to stretch a tin, and skip juice and cordial.

entries.name: Weight gain in the first weeks
aliases: how much weight should a newborn gain
entries.why: Nearly all babies lose a little weight in the first days and are back to birth weight by about two weeks. After that, steady gain along their own curve is what matters.
entries.whatToDo: Weigh at MCH visits rather than on the bathroom scales, and read the trend across weeks instead of one number. Bring the health record book to every appointment.

entries.name: Blood in vomit
entries.why: Blood in your baby's vomit needs a professional look today. It is sometimes swallowed blood from a cracked nipple, which is harmless, but that is not a call to make at home.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP now for a same day appointment. If there is a lot of blood, or your baby is pale, floppy or hard to rouse, ring 000.

entries.name: Let-down reflex
entries.why: Let down is the squeeze that pushes milk towards your baby. Some people feel a tingle or a deep ache, some feel nothing at all, and feeling nothing says nothing about supply.
entries.whatToDo: Warmth, a quiet spot and skin to skin all help it along. If it feels sharp or genuinely painful, mention it at your next check.

entries.name: Nipple confusion
entries.why: The evidence for nipple confusion is thin. Some babies do come to prefer the faster flow of a bottle, which is a technique issue rather than a one way door.
entries.whatToDo: If breastfeeding is going well, the odd bottle is unlikely to wreck it. Use paced bottle feeding, offer the breast first, and ring the ABA helpline if feeding changes.

entries.name: Oversupply and fast flow
aliases: baby chokes and pulls off the breast
entries.why: A forceful supply can leave your baby gulping, coughing, pulling off and windy, with frothy green poo. It is a real thing, not fussiness, and it usually settles by a few months.
entries.whatToDo: Try laid back feeding so gravity works against the flow, and finish one side before offering the other. Ring the ABA helpline on 1800 686 268 if it is not easing.

entries.name: Thrush
aliases: white patches in my babys mouth
entries.why: Shiny or flaky nipples with burning pain that carries on after the feed, often alongside white patches in your baby's mouth, can be thrush. You both need treating at the same time.
entries.whatToDo: See your GP so you and your baby are treated together. Wash and hot dry anything touching your breasts, change breast pads often, and keep feeding while you treat it.

entries.name: A baby you cannot console at all
entries.why: Normal crying still eases, even briefly, when you pick your baby up. Crying that nothing touches at all, for hours, in a baby who also seems unwell, needs to be looked at today.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your 24 hour nurse line or your GP now and say your baby cannot be consoled. If your baby is also floppy, pale, hot, cold, vomiting or breathing oddly, go to an emergency department.

entries.name: A weak or high-pitched cry
aliases: baby has gone quiet and whimpery
entries.why: A cry that is weak, high pitched or moaning, rather than loud and angry, can be a sign your baby is seriously unwell. This one is about the quality of the cry, not how long it has gone on.
entries.whatToDo: Ring 000 or go straight to the nearest emergency department. Describe the cry just as you hear it, and mention your baby's age, temperature, feeding and last wet nappy.

entries.name: Colic
entries.why: Colic is a description, not a disease: crying at least three hours a day, on three or more days a week, in a baby who is otherwise well and growing. It is grim, and it does end, usually by 3 to 4 months.
entries.whatToDo: Get it checked once so reflux, infection or allergy are ruled out, then focus on surviving it. Skip over the counter colic mixtures, and never let anyone do spinal manipulation on a baby.

entries.name: Crying peaks at 6 to 8 weeks
entries.why: There is good news hiding in bad news: crying usually peaks around 6 to 8 weeks and then falls away. By about 12 weeks most babies are down to roughly an hour a day. You are near the top of the hill.
entries.whatToDo: Mark that in your head and lower the bar on everything else for a fortnight. Swap shifts, accept help, and stop measuring yourself against a settled baby on the internet.

entries.name: Crying plus a fever
entries.why: A temperature of 38 degrees or higher in a baby under three months is always a reason to be seen, even if they otherwise look fine. Under one month old it means hospital, not the morning.
entries.whatToDo: Under 1 month, go to an emergency department now. Under 3 months, see a doctor today. Ring your 24 hour nurse line on the way if you want to talk it through. Do not give anything for fever without advice.

entries.name: Dummies for settling
entries.why: Sucking calms babies even when they are not hungry, so a dummy is a legitimate tool rather than a parenting failure. You can always drop it later, and plenty of babies drop it themselves.
entries.whatToDo: If you are breastfeeding, it is easier once feeding is established, often around 4 weeks. Offer it clean, never dip it in anything sweet, never tie it to your baby, and let it stay out if it falls out.

entries.name: How much crying is normal
entries.why: Newborns cry a lot, and it is not a sign you are doing it wrong. Two to three hours spread across a day is ordinary in the early weeks. It is their only way of saying something is up.
entries.whatToDo: Work the basics first: hungry, wind, tired, nappy, too warm. Then just comfort and hold. Crying with no cause you can find still counts as normal crying.

entries.name: Hunger cues
entries.why: Crying is the last stop on the hunger train, not the first. Stirring, turning the head, mouth opening, hands to mouth and sucking on anything all come earlier, and they are much easier to feed.
entries.whatToDo: Offer a feed as soon as you spot the early cues. If your baby is already roaring, calm them first with a cuddle and some skin to skin, then feed. Feeding to settle is completely fine.

entries.name: Needs a burp
entries.why: A sudden sharp cry, squirming, arching or legs drawn up right after a feed usually means wind. Not every baby needs burping, but the ones who do will tell you about it loudly.
entries.whatToDo: Hold them upright against your shoulder and pat or rub their back, or sit them on your lap leaning slightly forward. Two or three minutes is plenty. No burp is not a problem.

entries.name: Never shake a baby
entries.why: Shaking a baby, even once, even briefly, can cause bleeding in the brain, permanent disability or death. A newborn's neck cannot hold their head. If it has happened, your baby needs help straight away.
entries.whatToDo: Ring 000 now, even if your baby looks fine. Say what happened, because that is what gets your baby treated fast. If you are near that edge and have not acted on it, put your baby down and ring someone.

entries.name: The settling ladder
aliases: what to try when baby cries
entries.why: There is an order that works better than panic. Start with the body, then the senses, then movement, then you. Give each rung a couple of minutes before you climb to the next one.
entries.whatToDo: 1 Feed and burp. 2 Nappy and temperature. 3 Dim and quiet. 4 Wrap or hold firmly. 5 White noise. 6 Rock, sway or carry. 7 Something to suck. 8 Skin to skin. 9 Walk outside. 10 Hand over.

entries.name: The witching hour
entries.why: That late afternoon and evening stretch of grizzling is so common it has a nickname. Babies are tired and overstimulated by then, and milk supply is at its lowest point of the day. It passes with age.
entries.whatToDo: Plan for it instead of fighting it. Dinner early, lights down, a lap of the block in the carrier or pram, a bath, or more frequent feeds through the afternoon. Tag team if there are two of you.

entries.name: Tired cues
aliases: how do i know baby is tired
entries.why: Most 3am crying mysteries are just a baby who got past their window. Yawning, staring into space, jerky movements, grizzling, sucking on fingers and losing interest in you are the early signs.
entries.whatToDo: Start settling at the first yawn, not the third. Overtired babies fight sleep harder, so going early is easier than catching up. Newborns often only manage an hour or so awake at a time.

entries.name: When you cannot cope with the crying
aliases: at the end of my rope
entries.why: Reaching the end of your rope with a screaming baby does not make you a bad parent. It makes you an exhausted human. There is a safe plan for this exact moment, and using it is the right call.
entries.whatToDo: Put your baby on their back in the cot, shut the door and walk away. Breathe. Five or ten minutes of crying in a safe cot harms nobody. Then ring your MCH nurse, Lifeline on 13 11 14, or a friend.

entries.name: A cry that sounds wrong to you
entries.why: You have been listening to this baby day and night. If the cry has changed and something in you says this is not the usual, that is worth acting on. Parent instinct is real information.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your MCH nurse, or your 24 hour nurse line after hours, and say exactly that: the cry has changed and it does not sound right. Nobody will think you are overreacting.

entries.name: Crying plus vomiting or a rash
entries.why: Crying on its own is usually nothing. Crying with forceful or green vomiting, a rash that does not fade when pressed, or a baby who has gone off feeds is a different thing, and needs looking at today.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your 24 hour nurse line or your GP now. If a rash stays visible when you press a glass against it, or your baby is floppy or hard to wake, ring 000 instead.

entries.name: Movement and rocking
entries.why: Your baby spent nine months being jiggled, so motion switches something off. A sway, a carrier, a lap of the block with the pram or a bounce on a birth ball often does what standing still cannot.
entries.whatToDo: Hold them close and move from your knees, small and rhythmic rather than vigorous. If they fall asleep in a pram, carrier or car seat, move them to a flat safe surface when you can.

entries.name: Overstimulated baby
entries.why: After a big day of visitors, shops or cuddles, a newborn simply runs out of capacity. Turning the head away, jerky arms, clenched fists and a cry that comes out of nowhere are the tell.
entries.whatToDo: Strip the room back: lights low, phones away, one person, no talking. Hold them quietly or wrap them and expect a bit of crying as they come down. Quiet time before sleep helps a lot.

entries.name: Period of PURPLE crying
entries.why: PURPLE is only a memory aid for normal crying: Peak around two months, Unexpected, Resists soothing, Pain like face, Long lasting, Evening. It names what you are living through and says it is a phase.
entries.whatToDo: Use it as permission to stop hunting for a cause you cannot find. Resists soothing does not mean you failed. Keep holding, keep swapping out with someone, and let the weeks do the work.

entries.name: Skin to skin
entries.why: Bare chest to bare chest settles heart rate, breathing and temperature for both of you, and it keeps working well past the newborn weeks. It is the lowest effort trick in the book.
entries.whatToDo: Shirt off, baby in a nappy on your chest, a blanket over the two of you, and sit somewhere upright where you will not doze off. Dads and partners count exactly as much here.

entries.name: The five S's
entries.why: Swaddle, side or stomach hold in your arms, shush, swing and suck. It is a tidy way to remember what calms a newborn, because all together it feels a bit like being back inside.
entries.whatToDo: Do them at once, not one by one. Side and stomach holds are for your arms while awake only. Stop swaddling once your baby shows signs of rolling. Sleep is always on the back, every time.

entries.name: Too hot or too cold
entries.why: This one is quick to check and easy to get wrong in both directions. Feel the back of the neck or the chest, not the hands and feet, which are cool and a bit blue on most newborns.
entries.whatToDo: Aim for one more layer than you are comfortable in. A clammy neck, flushed face or damp hair means take a layer off. Keep the room around 18 to 22 degrees, no hats indoors, no doonas in the cot.

entries.name: What the cry might mean
aliases: what does my baby's cry mean
entries.why: Cries do have patterns, but nobody reads them perfectly, nurses included. Run the list rather than decoding the sound and you will be right most of the time.
entries.whatToDo: Find the closest match below. Unwell goes to the top of the list the moment anything else seems off, no matter what the cry sounds like.

variants.label: Short and rhythmic, builds up, with rooting or hands to mouth
variants.why: That is usually hunger. Newborns go from calm to furious fast, so a feed beats a stopwatch.
variants.whatToDo: Offer a feed even if the last one was recent. Cluster feeding in the evening is normal.

variants.label: Sharp and sudden, legs pulled up, going stiff
variants.why: Often wind, or the sheer effort of doing a poo. Babies strain and roar and then look delighted.
variants.whatToDo: Burp them upright, try knees to tummy bicycles, or lay them along your forearm.

variants.label: Whiny and grizzly, with yawning and a glazed stare
variants.why: Tired. An overtired baby fights sleep harder, so the window matters more than the clock.
variants.whatToDo: Dim, quiet, wrap if not rolling yet, and settle before the grizzle becomes a scream.

variants.label: Weak, high pitched or moaning, or nothing settles them at all
variants.why: This cry is different in kind, not in volume. It can mean your baby is unwell.
variants.whatToDo: Ring now and describe the sound. Do not wait for morning.

entries.name: A red, smelly or weeping cord
entries.why: A stump that is red around the base, smells bad, is weeping pus, or feels warm and tender needs treating. Infections here can move quickly in a newborn, so today matters.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP today, or your 24 hour nurse line after hours. If your baby also has a fever, is feeding poorly or seems unwell in themselves, go to an emergency department instead.

entries.name: Blood in poo or vomit
entries.why: Blood in poo or in vomit always gets looked at. The cause is often minor, like a small tear from a hard poo or a cracked nipple, but that is a call for a clinician to make rather than an app.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP today, or your 24 hour nurse line after hours. Keep the nappy. If there is a lot of blood, your baby is pale or floppy, or the vomit looks green, ring 000.

entries.name: Constipation
entries.why: Grunting, going red and straining is normal newborn work, not constipation. Real constipation means hard, dry, pellet like poo that hurts to pass, and it is rare in exclusively breastfed babies.
entries.whatToDo: Keep feeds up. A warm bath, gentle clockwise tummy massage and bicycle legs can help. Never use laxatives or put anything in the bottom without advice. Ring if there is blood or it drags on.

entries.name: Cord stump care
aliases: when does the cord fall off
entries.why: The stump dries out, darkens and drops off by itself, usually within one to two weeks. A bit of ooze or a sticky patch as it comes away is normal. Clean and dry is the entire job.
entries.whatToDo: Plain water and a soft cloth, then let it air. No antiseptic, no alcohol wipes, no creams. Fold the nappy down below it, and never pull it off, even when it is hanging by a thread.

entries.name: Days without a poo on breast milk
entries.why: A breastfed baby over about six weeks can go days, even up to a week, without a poo and be perfectly well. Breast milk is absorbed so completely that there is barely any waste left to pass.
entries.whatToDo: Check what actually matters: enough wet nappies, a soft tummy, a baby who is feeding and content, and soft poo when it does show up. Then relax, and have the spare clothes ready.

entries.name: Diarrhoea
entries.why: Breastfed poo is naturally sloppy, so runny is not automatically diarrhoea. The flag is a sudden change to very watery and much more frequent poo, often with vomiting. The real worry is dehydration.
entries.whatToDo: Keep feeding, more often and smaller if needed, with breast milk or formula rather than water or juice. Watch wet nappies closely. Ring your GP or your 24 hour nurse line if they drop off, or if there is blood.

entries.name: Green poo
aliases: why is my baby's poo green
entries.why: Green poo is one of the most googled nappies there is, and it is almost always fine. Green is simply a normal colour. A happy, feeding, growing baby with green poo needs nothing from you.
entries.whatToDo: Carry on. If every single poo is frothy green, your baby is unsettled and feeding is a struggle, it is worth a chat about attachment or supply with your MCH nurse or the ABA helpline.

entries.name: How many nappies a day
aliases: how many nappies will i need
entries.why: Plan on about 8 to 12 nappies a day in the newborn weeks, dropping to around 6 to 8 by a few months old. That is roughly 70 a week, which is why everyone tells you to buy in bulk.
entries.whatToDo: Buy one box of newborn size and more of the size above, because they grow out of newborn fast. Change at every feed and whenever there is poo, and do not wake a sleeping baby to check.

entries.name: How often they poo
entries.why: There is no single right number, and what counts as normal depends on what is going in. The texture, and how your baby is in themselves, matter far more than the count does.
entries.whatToDo: Find your situation below. In every case, soft poo plus a content growing baby plus enough wet nappies means things are working.

variants.label: Breastfed, first six weeks
variants.why: Usually three or more soft or runny poos a day, often one with every feed. Plenty is a good sign.
variants.whatToDo: Fewer than three a day in the first six weeks is worth raising with your MCH nurse.

variants.label: Breastfed, after six weeks
variants.why: Anything from several a day to one every few days, sometimes a week. Breast milk leaves little waste.
variants.whatToDo: As long as it is soft when it finally arrives, there is nothing to do.

variants.label: Formula fed
variants.why: Usually one to several a day, firmer, browner and smellier. Less often than breastfed is expected.
variants.whatToDo: Check your scoop measurements if poos turn hard or pellet like.

variants.label: Hard, dry, pellet like, or straining with blood
variants.why: That is constipation rather than just infrequent, and it is uncommon in exclusively breastfed babies.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your MCH nurse or GP, especially in a baby under 6 months.

entries.name: Meconium, the first poos
entries.why: That black green sticky tar in the first nappies is meconium, and it is meant to be there. It is what your baby built up before they were born. It usually clears in the first two or three days.
entries.whatToDo: Expect one or two in the first 24 hours. A smear of oil or barrier cream on a clean bottom makes it come off far more easily. If there is no poo at all by 48 hours, mention it to your midwife.

entries.name: Nappy rash
entries.why: Nearly every baby gets a red, sore bottom at some point, and it is not a sign of a dirty nappy or a slack parent. Most of it clears in a couple of days once the skin gets a break from wet.
entries.whatToDo: Change often, pat dry rather than rub, thick barrier cream at every change, and nappy free time on a towel. Ring your GP if it has not improved in a week, or if it blisters, crusts or spreads.

entries.name: Pale or chalky poo
entries.why: Pale, chalky, white or clay coloured poo is one of the few nappy findings that needs same day attention. It can mean bile is not getting through to the bowel. Picked up early, it is treatable.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP and ask to be seen today, not next week. Take a photo of the nappy in natural light, and bring the nappy itself if you can.

entries.name: The poo colour chart
aliases: what colour should baby poo be
entries.why: Most colours are fine. Mustard, green, brown and tan are all normal in a milk fed baby. Only three colours really matter: pale or chalky, red with blood, and black after the first few days.
entries.whatToDo: Match the colour below. Pale, bloody or black beyond the first days means ring today. Everything else, keep feeding and watch how your baby is in themselves rather than what is in the nappy.

variants.label: Mustard yellow, seedy and runny
variants.why: The classic breastfed poo. Loose, oddly sweet smelling, and often arriving with sound effects.

variants.label: Green, any shade
variants.why: Green is a normal colour, not a warning. It can be speed through the gut, a cold, or just today.

variants.label: Tan, brown, firmer
variants.why: Typical for formula fed babies, and for breastfed babies once solids start.

variants.label: Mucus, stringy or slimy bits
variants.why: A little mucus happens, often with dribble or a cold. Lots of it, or mucus with blood, needs checking.
variants.whatToDo: Mention it at your next visit, or sooner if your baby is unsettled or off feeds.

variants.label: Pale, chalky, white or grey
variants.why: Pale poo can mean bile is not reaching the bowel. That needs checking today, not next week.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your GP today. Photograph the nappy and take the nappy with you.

variants.label: Blood, red streaks, or like blackcurrant jam
variants.why: Blood in a nappy always gets assessed, even when the cause turns out to be a tiny tear.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your GP or your 24 hour nurse line today and keep the nappy.

variants.label: Black after the first few days
variants.why: Black is expected only while meconium clears. Later on it can mean digested blood.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your GP today and keep the nappy to show them.

entries.name: Wet nappies by day of life
entries.why: Wet nappies are the most reliable gauge you have at home of whether your baby is getting enough. Roughly one on day one, two on day two, and so on, settling at six or more a day from day five.
entries.whatToDo: From about day five, look for five or more heavy disposables, or six to eight wet cloth nappies, every 24 hours, with pale wee. Pop a tissue in the nappy on the days you cannot tell.

entries.name: A sunken soft spot
entries.why: The soft spot on top of your baby's head should look flat, or very slightly curved. A clear dip or hollow is a late sign of dehydration, and it needs to be seen straight away.
entries.whatToDo: Ring 000, or go to the nearest emergency department now. Keep offering feeds on the way. Do not wait to see whether it fills out again on its own.

entries.name: Baby boys: what is normal
entries.why: A swollen scrotum, erections and a foreskin that will not pull back are all normal newborn boy business. The foreskin is meant to be attached for the first few years, so it is not stuck.
entries.whatToDo: Wash the outside with water only and never force the foreskin back. Point the penis down in the nappy to save your walls. Ring your GP if the scrotum is red, hard, or sore when touched.

entries.name: Baby girls: what is normal
entries.why: In the first week or two, baby girls can have swollen genitals, thick white discharge and even a little vaginal bleeding. That is your hormones leaving her system, and it settles on its own.
entries.whatToDo: Wipe front to back with water and cotton wool or a plain wipe. Do not clean inside the labia or try to separate them. Ring your MCH nurse if bleeding is heavy, bright, or past the first fortnight.

entries.name: Black poo after the first days
entries.why: Black poo is normal only while meconium is clearing, in the first two or three days. Turning up later than that, it can mean blood that has been digested, so it needs a look.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP today and keep the nappy. Mention any iron drops your baby is taking, which can also turn poo very dark, and bring the bottle along so they can see the dose.

entries.name: Brick dust in the nappy
entries.why: A brick red, orange or pink powdery stain in the first few days is usually urate crystals in very concentrated wee, not blood. It is common while your milk is still coming in.
entries.whatToDo: Feed often and keep counting wet nappies. It should stop after about day four or five. If it keeps up past then, or wet nappies are dropping off, ring your MCH nurse today.

entries.name: How to change a nappy
entries.why: Nobody is born knowing this, and you will be quick at it within a week. The only real rule is that one hand stays on your baby the whole time, because they roll sooner than you expect.
entries.whatToDo: Gear within reach. Undo, scoop the worst with the front of the nappy, wipe front to back, pat dry, barrier cream, clean nappy with two fingers of room at the waist, folded below the cord.

entries.name: Mucus in the nappy
entries.why: A bit of clear or white slime in a nappy is common, often from swallowed dribble or a cold. A baby who is otherwise feeding and content does not need anything done about it.
entries.whatToDo: Keep an eye on it. If there is a lot of mucus, it keeps up for more than a few days, there is blood with it, or your baby goes off feeds, ring your MCH nurse or GP.

entries.name: Mustard yellow poo
entries.why: Mustard yellow, runny and a bit seedy, like grainy mustard, is exactly what breastfed poo is supposed to look like. It even smells surprisingly inoffensive. Nothing to do here at all.

entries.name: No tears when crying
entries.why: Many babies make few real tears in the first weeks, so on its own this is not alarming. In an older baby, or alongside fewer wet nappies and a dry mouth, it points towards dehydration.
entries.whatToDo: Count today's wet nappies first. If they are down, or your baby has a dry mouth, is sleepy or is not feeding, ring your 24 hour nurse line or your GP now rather than waiting for morning.

entries.name: When a nappy needs a doctor
entries.why: Most nappies need nothing but a wipe. The short list worth acting on is pale or chalky poo, blood, black poo after the first days, fewer wet nappies, watery poo with vomiting, and a red weeping cord.
entries.whatToDo: If any of those turn up, ring your MCH nurse, GP or your 24 hour nurse line today, and take a photo of the nappy. Everything else can safely wait for your next routine check.

entries.name: Eczema
entries.why: Eczema is dry, red, rough, itchy skin, often on the cheeks, in the elbow and knee creases and behind the ears. It flares and settles. Moisturiser is the groundwork, every single day.
entries.whatToDo: Moisturise generously twice a day, keep baths short and lukewarm, and use a soap free wash. See your GP or MCH nurse if it weeps, crusts, will not settle, or is wrecking sleep.

entries.name: Snuffly noisy breathing
entries.why: Newborn breathing is loud, snorty and irregular: fast bursts, a pause, then a sigh. Narrow nasal passages make the snuffle. A noisy baby who feeds well, with a soft, still chest, is fine.
entries.whatToDo: Saline drops before feeds if a blocked nose gets in the way. Ring 000 if breathing turns fast and laboured, ribs suck in, they grunt with each breath, or lips look blue.

entries.name: Sticky eye
aliases: eye glued shut in the morning
entries.why: Yellow or creamy crust in the corner of one eye, worst on waking, with a white eyeball and a comfortable baby, is usually a blocked tear duct rather than an infection.
entries.whatToDo: Wipe from the inner corner outwards with cotton wool and cooled boiled water, a fresh piece each wipe. See your GP if the white of the eye is red, the lid swells, or there is lots of pus.

entries.name: The first bath
aliases: when to give the first bath
entries.why: There is no rush. Hospitals now wait at least 24 hours, often longer, because the vernix is doing good work. Topping and tailing with a warm cloth is perfectly good for the early days.
entries.whatToDo: Warm room, water about 37 degrees tested with your elbow, only a few centimetres deep, everything in reach, and one hand on your baby the whole time. Never leave them, not for a second.

entries.name: Baby acne
entries.why: Small red pimples across the cheeks, nose and forehead often turn up around 2 to 4 weeks, courtesy of leftover hormones. It looks worse than it is and it fades over weeks without any treatment.
entries.whatToDo: Wash with plain water and pat dry. No acne products, no oils, no scrubbing. Ring your nurse if it weeps, crusts yellow, or spreads down the body.

entries.name: Baby nails
entries.why: Newborn nails are soft, grow fast, and come with built in face scratching. Filing is easier and safer than cutting in the early weeks, and a sleeping baby is a far more cooperative one.
entries.whatToDo: File, or use blunt baby scissors after a bath when nails are soft, straight across on fingers and toes. Mittens or long sleeves help overnight if their face is taking a beating.

entries.name: Blocked tear duct
entries.why: A tear duct that has not opened fully leaves one eye watery and often a bit crusty. It bothers you far more than it bothers your baby, and about nine in ten clear up before the first birthday.
entries.whatToDo: Wipe the eye clean, and if your nurse shows you how, massage gently along the side of the nose. Mention it at your checks so somebody is keeping track of it.

entries.name: Cradle cap
entries.why: Greasy yellow or white scales on the scalp, brows or behind the ears are cradle cap. It does not itch, it does not bother your baby, and it usually sorts itself out by the first birthday.
entries.whatToDo: Massage in a little plain oil, leave it a while, then wash and loosen the scales with a soft brush. Do not pick. Ring your nurse if it looks red, weepy or spreading.

entries.name: Dry peeling skin
entries.why: Newborns shed the top layer of skin in the first week or two, worst on the hands, feet and ankles. Babies born a little late peel the most. Underneath is perfectly good new skin.
entries.whatToDo: Short, warm baths a couple of times a week, and a plain unscented moisturiser if you like. No fragranced oils, and no picking or scrubbing the flakes off.

entries.name: Head shape and flat spots
entries.why: Newborn heads mould easily, so a flat patch on the side or back is common, especially if your baby always turns the same way. Most improve a lot once they start moving, and early action helps.
entries.whatToDo: Always back for sleep, then swap which end of the cot their head is at, change your feeding arm, and build up tummy time while awake. Ask your MCH nurse to check the shape and the neck.

entries.name: Heat rash
entries.why: Fine red or clear pinprick bumps in the skin folds, on the neck, chest and back, from blocked sweat glands on a warm day or one layer too many. It clears once your baby cools down.
entries.whatToDo: Take a layer off, move somewhere cooler, and let the skin breathe. Dress them as you are dressed plus one light layer for sleep, and feel the back of their neck to check.

entries.name: Hiccups
entries.why: Babies hiccup constantly, before birth and after it, and they genuinely do not mind. A diaphragm still learning its job plus a full tummy equals hiccups. They do not need stopping.
entries.whatToDo: Carry on with your day. A breastfeed or an upright cuddle often ends them. No water, no holding their nose, and absolutely no startling them.

entries.name: How often to bathe
aliases: how often should i bath my baby
entries.why: Two or three baths a week is plenty for a baby who does not get dirty in interesting places. Daily is fine too if you both enjoy it, as long as it is short and you moisturise afterwards.
