entries.whatToDo: Keep baths to about 5 to 10 minutes in lukewarm water, with a soap free wash or none at all. Clean the face, neck folds and nappy area every day regardless.

entries.name: Milia
entries.why: Those tiny firm white bumps across the nose, cheeks and chin are blocked oil glands. Nearly every newborn has a few, and they clear on their own over the first few weeks.
entries.whatToDo: Leave them alone. Do not squeeze or scrub them, and skip the creams. Plain water on a soft cloth is all their face actually needs.

entries.name: Newborn blotchy rash
entries.why: In the first week lots of newborns come out in blotchy red patches with a small white or yellow centre, and they move around the body overnight. It is harmless and it clears by itself.
entries.whatToDo: Nothing at all, and no creams. Ring your MCH nurse or GP if the spots blister, weep, turn into yellow crusts, or your baby goes off their feeds or feels feverish.

entries.name: Sneezing
entries.why: Newborns sneeze to clear lint, dust and milk out of very small nostrils. A run of sneezes with no runny nose, no cough, and a baby feeding happily is housekeeping, not a cold.
entries.whatToDo: Nothing. Start paying closer attention if sneezing arrives with a runny nose, a cough, a fever, or feeding that falls away, and ring your GP today if your baby is under 3 months.

entries.name: Soft spots on the head
entries.why: The soft spots let the skull flex and grow. The big one on top can take up to 18 months to close, and you may see it pulse with the heartbeat. Normal washing and handling will not hurt it.

variants.label: Soft, flat, moving with the heartbeat
variants.why: Exactly what a healthy fontanelle does. You can wash over it and brush the hair above it without a second thought.
variants.whatToDo: Nothing. Handle their head as you normally would and keep supporting the neck.

variants.label: Sunken and dipped in
variants.why: A soft spot that has sunk below the level of the skull usually means your baby is short of fluid.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your GP today and feed little and often. Ring 000 if they are floppy, hard to wake, or nappies have gone dry.

variants.label: Bulging, tight or firm
variants.why: A soft spot that bulges while your baby is calm and upright, especially with a fever, vomiting or sleepiness, is urgent.
variants.whatToDo: Ring 000 or go straight to the emergency department.

entries.name: Startle reflex
entries.why: The Moro reflex: arms and legs shoot out, then curl back in, at a noise, a light, or the feeling of falling as you put them down. It says the nervous system is wired up right, and it fades by about 4 months.
entries.whatToDo: Lower them bottom first and keep a hand on their chest a moment longer. If you swaddle for sleep, follow the Red Nose rules and stop as soon as they show any sign of rolling.

entries.name: Sun protection under 6 months
aliases: can i take baby to the beach
entries.why: Babies under 6 months should be kept out of direct sun altogether. Their skin burns fast and sunscreen is not the main tool at this age. Shade, clothing and timing do the heavy lifting.
entries.whatToDo: Shade, long sleeves, long pants and a broad brim hat, and plan outings early or late. Use a little baby sunscreen only where you cannot cover. Never drape a blanket over the pram.

entries.name: Swollen breasts or genitals
entries.why: Your hormones crossed the placenta, so newborn boys and girls can arrive with swollen breast buds, swollen genitals, a little milky discharge, or even a few spots of blood. It settles over weeks.
entries.whatToDo: Leave it be, and never squeeze a breast bud. Ring your GP if the area turns hot, hard and red, if redness is spreading, or if your baby has a fever or will not feed.

entries.name: Thrush in the nappy area
aliases: bright red rash in the creases
entries.why: Thrush is a yeast, not plain irritation. It shows as a bright red, shiny rash that runs into the deepest creases, with small spots scattered at the edges, and barrier cream alone will not shift it.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP today, because this needs an antifungal cream rather than more barrier cream. Check your baby's mouth and your own nipples too, since thrush travels.

entries.name: Birthmarks
entries.why: Most birthmarks are harmless and many fade on their own. What matters is where it sits, whether it is growing, and whether it bleeds or breaks open. A photo beside a ruler tracks it nicely.

variants.label: Flat pink, red or brown marks
variants.why: Flat marks, including the bluish grey patches often seen over the back and bottom, are just pigment or small blood vessels.
variants.whatToDo: Note where they are in your baby book, and mention them at your next nurse or GP visit.

variants.label: A raised red lump that is growing
variants.why: Strawberry marks often appear in the first weeks, grow for several months, then shrink away over the following years.
variants.whatToDo: Get your GP to look at it early, while it is still growing, so they can decide whether it needs any treatment.

variants.label: Near an eye, nose, mouth or nappy area, or bleeding
variants.why: A birthmark that could block sight or breathing, sits where it rubs, or breaks open and bleeds needs specialist advice now.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your GP today for a referral. Press gently with a clean cloth if it is bleeding.

entries.name: Bow legs and turned in feet
entries.why: Curved legs and inward turning feet are how a baby who has been folded up for months arrives. Legs straighten as they grow, and most feet sort themselves out once walking gets going.
entries.whatToDo: No special shoes, no bracing, no stretching. Have the hips and legs checked at your routine visits, and mention any difference you notice between the two sides.

entries.name: Dry or peeling lips
entries.why: Dry, peeling lips and the little sucking blister or callus in the middle of the top lip come with the job of feeding. They do not hurt, and they do not mean your baby is thirsty.
entries.whatToDo: Leave them, or dab on a smear of breastmilk or a plain balm. Ring your nurse if dry lips come with fewer wet nappies, since that points to fluid rather than friction.

entries.name: Stork bites and angel kisses
aliases: pink mark on back of neck
entries.why: A flat salmon pink patch on the back of the neck, the eyelids or between the brows is a stork bite. It flushes brighter when your baby cries or warms up, and most fade in the first year or two.
entries.whatToDo: Nothing. The ones on the face usually fade away, and the one on the neck may stay put and sit happily under hair forever.

entries.name: A floppy baby
entries.why: A baby who has gone limp, whose head and limbs flop when you lift them, or who has lost their usual grip and tone, is seriously unwell. This is not ordinary tiredness.
entries.whatToDo: Ring 000 now. Keep them with you on their back or side, keep them warm, and stay on the line with the operator.

entries.name: A rash that does not fade
aliases: rash that doesn't fade when pressed
entries.why: Press a clear glass firmly over the rash. Most rashes go pale under it. Flat red or purple spots, or bruise like blotches, that stay put can mean meningococcal infection, and that moves fast.
entries.whatToDo: Ring 000 now. Do not wait for a fever, a stiff neck, or more spots to appear before you act. Photograph the rash so you can show how quickly it has changed.

entries.name: Blue or grey lips and skin
entries.why: Blue or grey lips, tongue or face means your baby is not getting enough oxygen. Blue hands and feet alone in a warm, happy newborn are common and different. Around the mouth is urgent.
entries.whatToDo: Ring 000 now. Keep them with you, upright and warm, and do exactly what the operator tells you.

entries.name: Bronchiolitis and RSV
entries.why: Bronchiolitis is a chest infection in babies, usually from RSV. It starts like a cold, then moves to the chest around day 2 or 3, with a cough, a wheeze and harder work to breathe.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP today so someone can watch them breathe and feed. Day 3 to 5 is often the worst of it. Ring 000 for fast or laboured breathing, pauses, grunting or blue lips.

entries.name: Colds in a baby
entries.why: Babies catch a lot of colds, and most run their course in about a week with a runny nose, a cough and some grumpiness. Being miserable is normal. Struggling to breathe or to feed is not.
entries.whatToDo: Keep feeds small and frequent, and watch breathing and wet nappies. Ring your GP today if they are under 3 months, have a fever, or are feeding much less than usual.

entries.name: Cough
entries.why: A cough is how a baby clears their airway, and most come with a cold and settle over a week or two. What the cough sounds like, and how hard they are working to breathe, is what decides this.

variants.label: Cough with a cold, feeding well
variants.why: Loose, rattly coughs that arrive with a runny nose are usually just a virus doing the rounds.
variants.whatToDo: Keep feeds up, hold them upright for a while after feeding, and keep an eye on their breathing.

variants.label: Barking, seal like cough
variants.why: That bark is croup. It often sounds worst at night and the airway can tighten quickly in a baby.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your GP today, or 000 if they are struggling to breathe, going quiet, or turning blue.

variants.label: Cough with fast or laboured breathing
variants.why: A cough plus ribs sucking in, grunting or fast breathing means your baby is working too hard to breathe.
variants.whatToDo: Ring 000.

entries.name: Fever in a baby 3 months and over
entries.why: A fever is a sign the immune system is working, not an illness in itself. In a baby over 3 months who is feeding, alert and comfortable, the number alone is not the worry.
entries.whatToDo: Offer feeds often, keep them lightly dressed, and check on them. Ring your GP if it lasts more than 2 days, they are getting worse, or anything about them feels wrong to you.

entries.name: Fever in a baby under 3 months
entries.why: In a baby under 3 months, 38 degrees or more is always taken seriously. Little babies cannot show infection the way older ones do, so a fever needs a doctor to look at them today.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP now and ask to be seen today. After hours that means the emergency department, not waiting for morning. Do not give anything for the fever before they are checked.

entries.name: Gastro in a baby
entries.why: Gastro means vomiting, watery poo, or both, and babies lose fluid faster than anybody. Under 6 months, and especially under 3 months, they need a doctor rather than a wait and see.
entries.whatToDo: Keep offering small, frequent breastfeeds or formula. Ring your GP today. Ring 000 if they are floppy, hard to wake, have sunken eyes, or have not weed in 6 hours.

entries.name: Newborn jaundice
entries.why: Yellow skin and eyes are very common in the first week while a newborn clears bilirubin. The day it started, how deep it goes, and how they are feeding decide whether it is ordinary or not.

variants.label: Started in the first 24 hours
variants.why: Jaundice on day one is never the ordinary kind, and it needs assessing straight away rather than at the next visit.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your midwife, hospital or GP now. Go to the emergency department if you cannot reach any of them.

variants.label: Day 2 to 5, feeding and weeing well
variants.why: This is the usual pattern. It peaks around day 3 to 5 and then fades over the following week or two.
variants.whatToDo: Feed often, 8 to 12 times a day, and have your midwife or MCH nurse look at them. Ring if the yellow deepens or reaches the legs.

variants.label: Still yellow after 2 weeks
variants.why: Jaundice that lasts beyond 2 weeks needs a blood test to find out why, even in a baby who is thriving.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your GP or MCH nurse for a review this week, and mention the colour of their poo and their wee.

variants.label: Yellow plus sleepy, feeding badly or arching
variants.why: Deep jaundice in a baby who is hard to wake, feeding poorly, or arching their back is urgent.
variants.whatToDo: Ring 000 or go to the emergency department now.

entries.name: Signs of dehydration
aliases: no tears and a dry mouth
entries.why: Look for fewer than 4 wet nappies in a day, a dry mouth, no tears, a sunken soft spot, sunken eyes, cold hands and feet, or a baby who is flatter and sleepier than usual.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP today, or the emergency department after hours. Feed little and often while you wait. Ring 000 if they are floppy, hard to wake, or breathing fast.

entries.name: Trust your gut
aliases: i just know something is off
entries.why: You know your baby better than any checklist does. If something feels wrong, that is reason enough to ring. Nobody will think you are overreacting, and nurses would far rather you called.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your 24 hour nurse line or your MCH nurse now and say what has changed. If your baby is hard to wake, floppy, blue or breathing badly, ring 000 instead.

entries.name: What counts as a fever
entries.why: A fever is 38 degrees or more. Below that is not a fever. What matters more than the number is your baby's age and how they are in themselves: feeding, alertness, breathing, colour.

variants.label: Baby under 3 months
variants.why: Any reading of 38 degrees or more needs a doctor today, even if your baby seems settled in themselves.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your GP now and ask for a same day appointment. After hours, go to the emergency department.

variants.label: Baby 3 months and over
variants.why: A fever on its own is the body doing its job. How your baby looks and feeds tells you more than the thermometer does.
variants.whatToDo: Offer extra feeds, keep them lightly dressed, and recheck. Ring your GP if it lasts more than 2 days or they get worse.

variants.label: Fever with any red flag
variants.why: A fever alongside a rash that does not fade, fast or laboured breathing, floppiness, or a baby you cannot wake is urgent.
variants.whatToDo: Ring 000.

entries.name: Who to ring after hours
entries.why: At 3am you still have options: a 24 hour nurse line, an after hours home visiting doctor, the hospital emergency department, and 000. You do not have to work out which illness it is first.
entries.whatToDo: Ring the nurse line and describe what you can see. For a baby under 3 months with a fever, or any red flag, skip the queue and go to the emergency department or ring 000.

entries.name: Will not wake properly
entries.why: Babies sleep deeply, but you should always be able to rouse them enough to feed or to protest. A baby who stays floppy and unfocused, or who you cannot wake at all, needs help now.
entries.whatToDo: Try undressing them and talking to them. If they do not properly wake, ring 000. If they wake but will not feed at all, ring your GP today.

entries.name: Working hard to breathe
entries.why: Fast breathing, ribs or the dip at the base of the neck sucking in, the head bobbing, grunting with each breath, flaring nostrils, or pauses. Any one of these means your baby is in trouble now.
entries.whatToDo: Ring 000. Keep them upright and with you, loosen tight clothing, and stay on the line. Do not drive yourself anywhere if they are getting worse while you watch.

entries.name: After immunisations
entries.why: Expect a grumpy, sleepy, off colour baby for a day or two, a mild fever, and a red, warm, tender spot where the needle went. That is the immune system doing exactly what it was asked to do.

variants.label: Grumpy, sleepy, mild fever, sore leg
variants.why: Common and expected in the first 48 hours. Extra cuddles and extra feeds are pretty much the whole treatment.
variants.whatToDo: Feed often, dress them lightly, and move the leg gently. Ask your nurse or pharmacist before giving anything for the pain.

variants.label: Fever past 48 hours, or redness spreading
variants.why: Reactions should be settling by day 3. A fever still going, or redness spreading out from the site, wants a look.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your MCH nurse or GP today, and tell them which immunisations were given and when.

variants.label: Under 3 months with any fever after needles
variants.why: A fever in a baby under 3 months is handled the same way whether or not they have just had their immunisations.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your GP now for a same day appointment, or the emergency department after hours.

variants.label: Floppy, pale, swollen face or trouble breathing
variants.why: These are signs of a serious reaction, and they need emergency help rather than a phone call to the clinic.
variants.whatToDo: Ring 000.

entries.name: Blocked nose
entries.why: Babies breathe through their nose, so a blocked one makes feeding hard work. Saline drops or spray before a feed loosen things up. No decongestants and no vapour rubs for babies.
entries.whatToDo: Try a couple of saline drops in each nostril before feeds, and offer shorter, more frequent feeds. Ring your MCH nurse or GP if they cannot feed or they are breathing hard.

entries.name: Croup and a barking cough
entries.why: Croup is a virus that swells the airway just below the voice box, giving a barking cough and a harsh noise breathing in. A baby's airway is small, so it can tighten fast, often at night.
entries.whatToDo: Stay calm and hold them upright, because crying makes it worse. Ring your GP today, or the emergency department after hours. Ring 000 if they struggle to breathe or go blue.

entries.name: Fast breathing
entries.why: Newborns breathe quickly and unevenly when awake, and that is normal. Steady fast breathing while they are calm or asleep, over about 60 breaths a minute, is not, and needs checking today.
entries.whatToDo: Count the breaths for a full minute while they are settled, and watch the chest and ribs. Ring your GP today. Ring 000 if ribs suck in, they grunt, or their lips look blue.

entries.name: Febrile convulsion
entries.why: A fever can set off a convulsion: stiffening, jerking, rolled eyes, no response. It is terrifying to watch and usually stops within a few minutes. A first one in a baby always gets checked.
entries.whatToDo: Lay them on their side on something soft, clear the space, nothing in their mouth, and note the time it started. Ring 000. Stay with them until they are properly awake.

entries.name: Grunting with each breath
aliases: noise at the end of each breath
entries.why: Grunting at the end of every breath is a baby trying to hold their lungs open. It is a different thing from the grunty, straining noises babies make while they sleep or pass wind.
entries.whatToDo: If the grunt comes with every breath, ring 000 now. Sleep grunts and straining noises in a baby who is otherwise settled, feeding and pink are common and not this.

entries.name: How to take a temperature
entries.why: Under the arm is the easiest and most reliable spot at home. Hold the digital probe snug in the armpit with the arm down until it beeps. Ear and forehead readings are less reliable in little babies.
entries.whatToDo: Write down the number and the time, plus how your baby is feeding and how alert they are. That second part is what the nurse or doctor will ask about first.

entries.name: Mottled or marbled skin
entries.why: A cold newborn can go briefly blotchy and marbled, and it clears as they warm up. Mottled, pale or grey skin in a baby who is unwell, floppy or feeding poorly is a sign of serious illness.
entries.whatToDo: Warm them gently and look again. If the mottling stays, or they are unwell, hard to rouse, or breathing badly, ring 000.

entries.name: Pauses in breathing
entries.why: Newborns breathe in bursts, so a pause of a few seconds followed by normal breathing is common. A pause longer than about 15 seconds, or any pause with colour change or floppiness, is not.
entries.whatToDo: Ring 000. If they are blue, limp or not responding, start infant CPR if you know it, and let the operator talk you through it step by step.

entries.name: Ribs sucking in
entries.why: When the skin pulls in under the ribs, between them, or at the base of the neck with every breath, your baby is using muscles they should not need. That is respiratory distress.
entries.whatToDo: Ring 000 now. Hold them upright, keep their clothing loose, and keep talking to the operator until help arrives.

entries.name: Teething
entries.why: Teething brings drool, chewing, red gums, a grizzly baby and broken sleep, usually from around 6 months. What it does not cause is a high fever, vomiting, diarrhoea, or a rash on the body.
entries.whatToDo: Offer something cool and firm to chew, and wipe the dribble so the chin stays happy. If there is a fever, treat it as illness, not teeth. Any fever under 3 months means ringing today.

entries.name: Wheezing
entries.why: A wheeze is a high whistling sound as your baby breathes out, and it means the small airways are narrowed. In a baby under 12 months that always deserves a doctor's ear today.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP for a same day appointment, or the emergency department after hours. Ring 000 if breathing is fast or laboured, they are grunting, or their lips look blue.

entries.name: Green or bloody vomit
entries.why: Bright or dark green vomit can mean the bowel is blocked. Blood in the vomit, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds, also needs urgent eyes on your baby rather than a wait.
entries.whatToDo: Ring 000 or go straight to the emergency department. Hold off on more feeds until someone has seen them, and take a photo of the vomit or keep the cloth to show.

entries.name: Pale poo with dark wee
entries.why: Chalky, pale or white poo with dark yellow or brown wee in a yellow baby can mean the liver or bile ducts need attention. Picked up early it is very treatable, so timing really matters.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP or MCH nurse today and ask for a jaundice review. Keep the nappy, or photograph it in daylight, so they can see the colour for themselves.

entries.name: First real smile
entries.why: The proper social smile, the one aimed at you, usually turns up around 6 weeks, and anywhere from 4 to 10 weeks is normal. The sleepy half smiles before that are real too, just not about you yet.
entries.whatToDo: Smile first and wait. Get close, catch their eye, and give them a few seconds to answer. It is the best unpaid work you will ever do.

entries.name: Fussy periods and leaps
entries.why: Just before a new skill lands, a lot of babies turn clingy, cranky and hopeless at sleep for a week or two. It is not a regression in anything, and it is not something you caused.
entries.whatToDo: Drop your expectations, hold them more, and keep the basics steady. If it drags on past a couple of weeks, or they seem unwell with it, get them checked.

entries.name: Milestones are ranges, not deadlines
entries.why: Every milestone age you read is the middle of a wide window, not a due date. Healthy babies reach the same skills months apart. What matters is that new skills keep showing up, not the week they land.
entries.whatToDo: Compare your baby to themselves last month, not to the baby at playgroup. Your MCH nurse checks development at every visit, so bring any worry straight there.

entries.name: Not meeting a milestone
entries.why: Late inside the normal range is just late. Past the top end of the range, with nothing new arriving either, is worth a proper look. That look is a check, not a verdict.
entries.whatToDo: Write down what they can and cannot do, then book a development check with your MCH nurse. Bring your child health record book so the whole picture is in front of them.

entries.name: Percentiles, weight and length
entries.why: A percentile is just where your baby sits in a crowd of 100, not a score. The tenth is not failing and the ninetieth is not winning. A baby who keeps following their own curve is doing it right.
entries.whatToDo: Look at the shape of the line across visits, not at today's dot. Length and head size get plotted the same way, and your nurse is reading the trend, not the number.

entries.name: Rolling over
entries.why: Most babies roll between 4 and 7 months, often tummy to back first. The day it happens two things change: the change table is no longer safe to turn your back on, and swaddling has to stop.
entries.whatToDo: Stop swaddling at the first sign of rolling, and keep putting them down on their back. Once they roll both ways let them find their own position. Never leave them alone up high.

entries.name: Tummy time progress
entries.why: Early tummy time is often 30 seconds of protest. That counts. Over the first few months it builds to lifting the head, then up on the forearms, then pushing the chest clear of the floor.
entries.whatToDo: Short and often beats long and miserable. A minute or two a few times a day while they are awake and you are watching, and try it on your chest if the floor is unpopular.

entries.name: Weight gain
entries.why: Newborns lose weight before they gain it, then most settle into steady gains. The shape of the line across several weigh ins tells you far more than any single number on the scales.
entries.whatToDo: Weigh at the nurse rather than at home, and on the same scales where you can. Bring the health record book to every visit so the whole pattern is visible.

variants.label: The first fortnight
variants.why: Losing up to about 10 per cent of birth weight in the first days is expected, and most babies are back to their birth weight by around 2 weeks old.
variants.whatToDo: Feed often, count the wet nappies, and keep the weigh in appointments.

variants.label: After the first fortnight
variants.why: Gains vary week to week, so one flat week is not a crisis. A line that flattens off or drops across two or more weigh ins needs a feeding review.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your MCH nurse, and the ABA helpline on 1800 686 268 if it is a breastfeeding question.

entries.name: Cooing and babbling
entries.why: Vowel sounds like ooh and aah start around 2 to 3 months. Consonants join in near 6 months and turn into babababa and dadada. It is practice, and it needs an audience.
entries.whatToDo: Copy their sounds back and then leave a gap. That back and forth is how conversation gets built, long before any word means anything.

entries.name: Corrected age for prem babies
entries.why: A baby born 8 weeks early gets measured against their due date, not their birthday. So at 6 months old they are doing 4 month things, and for them that is exactly on time.
entries.whatToDo: Use corrected age for milestones through the first 2 years or so, and keep every follow up appointment the hospital gives you. Say the corrected age out loud when people compare.

entries.name: Crawling
entries.why: Crawling is the one milestone plenty of babies skip altogether. What matters is that they find some way to get across the room, not that it looks like the crawl in the book.
entries.whatToDo: Give them floor time and something worth travelling for. Once they are mobile, go round the house at their eye level and sort the stairs, cords and small objects.

variants.label: Crawling, shuffling, commando or rolling
variants.why: Any method counts. Hands and knees crawling usually shows up between 6 and 10 months, but bum shuffling, commando crawling and rolling across the room are all normal ways to get around.
variants.whatToDo: Let them use whatever works and keep the floor interesting.

variants.label: Not moving anywhere by around 12 months
variants.why: Skipping crawling is fine. Showing no interest in getting anywhere by about 12 months, or only ever using one side of the body, is worth a proper look.
variants.whatToDo: Book a development check with your MCH nurse or GP and describe exactly what you are seeing.

entries.name: First teeth
entries.why: The bottom front two usually arrive around 6 to 10 months, though some babies are born with a tooth and some reach their first birthday with none. Both ends of that range are normal.
entries.whatToDo: Something cool and firm to chew on helps. Start brushing with a soft brush and water as soon as the first tooth is through, and skip teething gels and amber necklaces.

entries.name: First words
entries.why: A first real word, used on purpose and meaning the same thing twice, usually lands between 10 and 14 months. Mum and dad often get said long before they are aimed at anyone.
entries.whatToDo: Narrate your day, name whatever they are looking at, and answer their sounds as though they were words. Understanding always runs well ahead of speaking.

entries.name: Following things with their eyes
entries.why: By 6 to 8 weeks most babies lock onto your face and follow it as it moves. Early on the tracking is jerky and keeps losing the target, which is practice rather than a problem.
entries.whatToDo: Move your face slowly side to side about 25cm away and let them find you. No toy beats a real face at this age.

entries.name: Head control
aliases: when can baby hold head up
entries.why: A newborn head needs supporting every time you lift them. Most babies hold it steady for short bursts by 3 to 4 months and have it sorted by 6 months, as the neck strength builds.
entries.whatToDo: Support the head and neck whenever you lift or carry them, and keep tummy time going, because that is where those neck muscles get built.

entries.name: Pulling up to stand
entries.why: Most babies haul themselves up on the lounge somewhere between 8 and 12 months, then side step along it holding on. Standing usually runs weeks or months ahead of walking.
entries.whatToDo: Lower the cot base before they can pull up in it, and check what will tip over if they grab it. Bare feet grip better than socks on floorboards.

entries.name: Signs they are ready for solids
entries.why: Look for three things together: good head and trunk control sitting with support, real interest in your food, and reaching or opening up for the spoon. Age on its own is not the signal.
entries.whatToDo: Wait for the signs rather than the date, and have a word with your MCH nurse if none of them have turned up by about 7 months.

entries.name: Sitting up
entries.why: Propped sitting with help comes first, often around 4 to 6 months. Sitting steady without hands is usually 6 to 9 months. Expect plenty of slow topples on the way through.
entries.whatToDo: Sit them between your legs or ring them with cushions while they practise, and stay within arm's reach. Floor time does more for this than any seat.

entries.name: What a newborn can hear
entries.why: Hearing works before birth, so your voice is already familiar. Newborns turn towards sound, settle at a low steady voice and startle at a bang. Most babies get a hearing screen in the first few days.
entries.whatToDo: Talk, sing and read to them from day one. If the newborn hearing screen got missed or needs a repeat, chase it up with your MCH nurse.

entries.name: What a newborn can see
entries.why: About 20 to 30cm, which is roughly your face at a feed. They go for faces, strong contrast and movement, and they will not see fine detail or the full range of colour for months yet.
entries.whatToDo: Hold your face close when you talk to them, and give them something to look at rather than something to look through. Vision sharpens a lot by 3 months.

entries.name: Floppy or stiff baby
entries.why: A baby who has gone limp, will not wake properly or feels unusually stiff needs help now. Floppiness or stiffness that has been there a while still needs a doctor, just not an ambulance.
entries.whatToDo: Ring 000 now if they are limp, hard to rouse, grey or blue, or breathing strangely. If it has been there a while and they are otherwise well, ring your GP today.

entries.name: Grabbing and holding things
aliases: when can baby hold a toy
entries.why: Newborns grip anything in their palm by reflex. Deliberate grabbing turns up around 3 to 4 months, and picking up something small between finger and thumb is closer to 9 to 12 months.
entries.whatToDo: Offer something light and easy to hold within reach. Expect your hair, necklaces and skin to be grabbed with surprising force.

entries.name: Head circumference
entries.why: The head gets measured at every check because the brain is growing fastest now. Plenty of heads sit on a different line to the weight, and that is fine. It is the curve being watched.
entries.whatToDo: Keep the measurements going at every visit. Ring your nurse or GP today if the head seems to be growing very fast, the soft spot bulges or sinks, or they are vomiting and very drowsy.

entries.name: Losing a skill they had
entries.why: A skill that was solid and has now gone, like babbling that stopped, eye contact that faded, or sitting they can no longer do, is the one developmental sign that should not wait.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP today and ask for the first appointment about a lost skill. If you cannot get in, ring healthdirect on 1800 022 222 for advice on how soon to be seen.

entries.name: Not making eye contact
entries.why: Newborns look away a lot, and that is normal. By around 3 months most babies hold your gaze and follow your face. A baby who consistently does not look at faces needs checking.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your MCH nurse and ask for a development and vision check, or healthdirect on 1800 022 222 if the centre is shut. Say how long you have noticed it for.

entries.name: Not responding to sound
entries.why: Babies startle at sudden noise from birth and turn towards voices over the first months. No reaction to sound, or babbling that stops, needs a hearing check even if the newborn screen passed.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your MCH nurse today and ask for a hearing assessment referral, or healthdirect on 1800 022 222 after hours. A screen that passed does not rule it out.

entries.name: Staring at their own hands
entries.why: Somewhere around 2 to 4 months they discover their hands and find them riveting. It looks odd and it is a real milestone: they are working out that those things belong to them.
entries.whatToDo: Let them get on with it. Hands go to the mouth next, and that is exploration, not always hunger.

entries.name: Baby blues
aliases: crying for no reason after birth
entries.why: Around day 3 to 5, as the hormones drop and your milk comes in, plenty of people cry at nothing, feel raw, and wobble between joy and dread. It usually settles inside a week or two.
entries.whatToDo: Eat, sleep when you can, and tell your partner and your midwife how you actually feel. If it is still there after two weeks, or getting heavier, ring your GP. That is a different thing.

entries.name: Bleeding after birth
aliases: how long does bleeding last after birth
entries.why: Everyone bleeds after birth, caesarean included. It starts heavy and red, usually like a strong period, then fades to brown and then pale over 2 to 6 weeks. A gush when you stand up is common.
entries.whatToDo: Maternity pads rather than tampons, and no swimming until it stops. If it gets heavier again instead of lighter, or it starts to smell bad, ring your midwife or GP.

entries.name: Caesarean recovery
entries.why: It is major abdominal surgery, and you are recovering from it while lifting a baby. Six weeks is the usual guide, but the tiredness and the pulling at the scar often last longer than anyone warned you.
entries.whatToDo: Roll to your side to get up, hold a pillow when you cough, and hand over the lifting. Ring your GP today if the wound is red, hot, oozing or opening, or you have a fever.

entries.name: It is hard, and that is normal
aliases: is it supposed to be this hard
i feel like a bad mum
entries.why: You can love your baby completely and still find this the hardest thing you have ever done. Both being true at once is not a warning sign. It is what the newborn months are actually like.
entries.whatToDo: Say it out loud to someone who will not flinch. If the heaviness sits on you most of the day for more than two weeks, that is a GP appointment, not a character flaw.

entries.name: Perineal recovery
entries.why: Swelling, stinging and dreading the first wee are standard for a week or two. Stitches dissolve on their own and the worst of the soreness eases over a few weeks, though sitting comfortably takes longer.
entries.whatToDo: Ice packs, a squeeze bottle of warm water while you wee, and lying down beats sitting. Ring your GP or midwife if pain climbs after day 3, or there is smelly discharge or a fever.

entries.name: Postnatal depression and anxiety
entries.why: If flatness, dread, constant worry, panic, crying or feeling nothing has gone on for more than two weeks, that is postnatal depression or anxiety. It is common, it is an illness, and it is treatable.
entries.whatToDo: Ring PANDA on 1300 726 306 and book a GP appointment this week. Take your partner in with you. You do not need the right words ready, just turn up and say you are not okay.

entries.name: Rage and overwhelm
entries.why: Hours of crying can push a calm person to fury. Feeling a surge of rage does not make you a monster, it makes you a human who has not slept. What you do in the next minute is the part that matters.
entries.whatToDo: Put the baby safely in the cot, shut the door, and walk away for a few minutes. Never shake a baby. If this keeps happening or frightens you, ring your GP or PANDA on 1300 726 306.

entries.name: Shift sleeping
aliases: how to get a block of sleep
entries.why: Both of you waking for every feed just makes two wrecked people. Splitting the night into shifts means one of you gets a real unbroken stretch, and that is the bit that actually restores you.
entries.whatToDo: Pick the blocks, say 8pm to 2am and 2am to 8am, and the off duty one sleeps elsewhere with earplugs. Swap which shift you take so nobody always copes with the hard one.

entries.name: Sleep deprivation
entries.why: Weeks of broken sleep do real damage. Your memory goes, small things feel enormous, and you cry or snap at nothing. That is not weakness and it is not a character flaw. It is a sleep debt.
entries.whatToDo: Protect one block of 4 or 5 hours each night by taking turns, and sleep when they sleep once a day. If you are nodding off driving or while holding the baby, tell someone today.

entries.name: The first two weeks
aliases: what are the first weeks like
entries.why: The first fortnight is survival, not parenting. Your hormones crash, your body is healing, the baby feeds constantly, and day and night blur into one. Nobody is calm and capable in this bit.
entries.whatToDo: Lower the bar to fed, slept and held. Let the house go, say yes to food, and keep your midwife or MCH nurse visits, because that is where the small worries get sorted.

entries.name: Who does what at night
entries.why: If one of you is breastfeeding, the other can still do everything around it: the nappy, the resettle, the bottle, the glass of water, the pillow. Feeding is not the whole of the job.
entries.whatToDo: Agree it out loud before bedtime, not at 3am: who gets up first, who does the resettle, who takes the early morning so the other can sleep in. Write it on the fridge if you have to.

entries.name: Your relationship and the scorekeeping
entries.why: Most couples fight more in the first year. You are both exhausted, both doing more than you ever have, and both quietly certain you are doing more than the other. The tally in your head is not evidence.
entries.whatToDo: Swap jobs for a night so you each see the other's load. Have the hard conversation in daylight and fed, not at 3am. Book a counsellor early if it is not shifting.

entries.name: Afterpains
entries.why: Those period like cramps that grip while you feed are your uterus shrinking back, helped along by the hormone that releases your milk. Strongest in the first few days, and worse after a second baby.
entries.whatToDo: Wee before you feed, use a warm pack, and ask your midwife or pharmacist what pain relief suits you while feeding. Ring your GP if the pain is severe or keeps building.

entries.name: Asking for help
aliases: i need help with the baby
entries.why: Nobody was ever meant to do this with two people and no sleep. Asking is not failing, and most people genuinely want a job. They just need to be told which one it is.
entries.whatToDo: Ask for something specific: a cooked meal, a load of washing, an hour with the baby while you sleep. Your MCH nurse can also point you at local groups and sleep and settling services.

entries.name: Contraception after birth
aliases: can i get pregnant while breastfeeding
entries.why: You can get pregnant again sooner than you would think, including before any period comes back. What suits you depends on whether you are breastfeeding and on what you used before.
entries.whatToDo: Raise it at the 6 week check, or earlier if sex is back on the table. Your GP or a family planning clinic will walk you through the options.

variants.label: If you are breastfeeding
variants.why: Breastfeeding lowers your fertility, but it is not reliable contraception unless some very strict conditions are all met. Plenty of methods are fine while feeding, and some are not.
variants.whatToDo: Ask your GP which options suit breastfeeding, before you need them.

variants.label: If you are not breastfeeding
variants.why: Fertility can return within about 3 weeks of birth, so cover is worth sorting out before the 6 week check rather than at it.
variants.whatToDo: Ring your GP and ask what you can start now.

entries.name: Feeding your own self
entries.why: You will hit 2pm and realise all you have had is a cup of cold tea. Underfed and dehydrated makes every other part of this harder, and breastfeeding makes you hungrier and thirstier than you expect.
entries.whatToDo: Stash one handed food wherever you feed: nuts, crackers, cheese, fruit, a big water bottle. Accept every meal anyone offers, and cook double whenever you cook at all.

entries.name: Getting outside
aliases: can i take the baby outside
entries.why: A newborn can go outside from day one, weather and shade permitting. Ten minutes of daylight and a lap of the block does more for how you feel than another hour on the lounge.
entries.whatToDo: Keep the bar low: pram, pyjama pants, around the block. Use a proper pram shade rather than draping a cloth over it, which traps heat, and go back to bed afterwards if you need to.

entries.name: Heavy bleeding after birth
entries.why: Soaking a maternity pad in an hour or less, passing clots bigger than a golf ball, or feeling faint, dizzy or breathless means you need help now. Heavy bleeding after birth can turn serious fast.
entries.whatToDo: Ring 000 now. Lie down, keep the pad on so they can see how much blood there is, and have someone stay with you and take the baby.

entries.name: Intrusive thoughts
entries.why: Sudden horrifying images of your baby being hurt are far more common than anyone says, and deeply frightening. They are a symptom, not a plan, they do not make you dangerous, and they settle with help.
entries.whatToDo: Say it out loud to your GP, or ring PANDA on 1300 726 306. If any part of you feels like acting on a thought, ring 000 or Lifeline on 13 11 14 now.

entries.name: Partners struggle too
entries.why: Around one in ten dads and non birthing partners get depression or anxiety in the first year. It often shows up as anger, working late, drinking more or going quiet, rather than as sadness.
entries.whatToDo: Ask directly, and mean it. PANDA on 1300 726 306 is for partners too, and a GP appointment is the same first step. Do not wait for them to raise it first.

entries.name: Returning to exercise
aliases: when can i exercise after birth
entries.why: Walking and gentle pelvic floor work can start early. Running, jumping and heavy lifting need a healed pelvic floor and core, and that takes longer than feeling ready does.
entries.whatToDo: Start pelvic floor exercises as soon as you comfortably can, and build up the walking. Get cleared at your 6 week check, and see a pelvic health physio before you run.

variants.label: After a vaginal birth
variants.why: Gentle walking and pelvic floor exercises can start in the first weeks. Most people get cleared for more at the 6 week check, with high impact left until around 12 weeks.
variants.whatToDo: Stop and get checked if you leak, feel heaviness or dragging, or have pain.

variants.label: After a caesarean
variants.why: Your abdominal wall is healing from surgery, so leave the heavy lifting and any core work until your doctor clears you, usually at 6 weeks or later.
variants.whatToDo: Ask your GP at the 6 week check what you can add, and build back slowly.

entries.name: Signs of infection after birth
entries.why: A fever of 38 degrees or more, shivering, a wound that is hot, red or oozing, discharge that smells bad, burning wee, or pain that is getting worse instead of better all point to infection.
entries.whatToDo: Ring your GP or your maternity unit today, and 000 if you feel very unwell, confused, or cannot stop shivering. Infections after birth need treating early.

entries.name: The 6 week postnatal check
aliases: what happens at the six week check
entries.why: Around 6 weeks you and the baby both get checked, usually at the GP. Yours covers bleeding, stitches or the scar, blood pressure, mood, contraception, and whatever is still not right.
entries.whatToDo: Book it before you leave hospital if you can, and keep a list of questions in your phone as they come up. It is your appointment too, not just the baby's.

entries.name: Thoughts of harming yourself or the baby
entries.why: If you are thinking about hurting yourself or the baby, you need someone with you now. This happens to people who love their babies, and it can be treated. Telling someone is what changes it.
entries.whatToDo: Ring 000, or Lifeline on 13 11 14, or PANDA on 1300 726 306. Put the baby somewhere safe like the cot, and get another adult to you.

entries.name: Visitors and boundaries
entries.why: You are allowed to say not today. A visitor who holds the baby while you make them tea is costing you, and a newborn does not need an audience, least of all anyone with a cold.
entries.whatToDo: Pick your rules and let your partner be the one who says them: short visits, bring food, wash hands, nobody unwell, and we might not answer the door. No explanation owed.
